title: Original NCP-OUSD practice questions
notes: Original questions written for this workspace and tagged with study-guide objective numbers. They are not taken from the NVIDIA study guide or any exam dump. USDA-based answers are pinned by verify blocks that compose the layers with OpenUSD.

questions.stem: The layers below are opened with shot.usda as the root layer. What is the composed value of /World/Lamp.intensityScale?
options: 4, because opinions from both arcs are added together
No value, because class prims are abstract and never contribute opinions
explanations: The prim inherits </_class_Lamp>, and the class in the root layer stack authors 3. Inherits sit above references in LIVERPS, so the class opinion wins.
Attribute values are never summed across arcs; value resolution picks the single strongest opinion.
Class prims are skipped by default traversal, but their opinions still flow into every prim that inherits them.
The referenced asset does author 1, but a reference is weaker than an inherit arc on the same prim, so its opinion loses.

questions.stem: In shot.usda an artist selects the "blue" paint variant on /World/Car, yet paintName still reads "factory". What explains this?
options: "factory" is a schema fallback value, and fallbacks cannot be changed by variants.
A variant selection authored in a referencing layer is ignored; only the asset's own selection counts.
Variant opinions can only affect child prims, never properties of the prim that owns the variant set.
In car.usda, paintName is authored directly on Car outside the variant set; that direct opinion is stronger than any opinion inside a variant of the same layer stack.
explanations: paintName is a custom attribute with an authored value; schema fallbacks are only used when no opinion is authored at all.
The selection in shot.usda is honored (the composed selection is "blue"). Stronger layers are exactly where shot-level variant choices belong.
Variants may hold opinions on the owning prim's own properties as well as on descendants.
Within car.usda's layer stack, local (direct) opinions beat variant opinions, so the variant can never override "factory". Moving the default value into a variant (or removing it) fixes this.

questions.stem: bolt.usda is referenced into shot.usda as shown. What is the composed roughness of /World/Bolt/Looks/PolishedSteel?
options: No value, because specializes arcs cannot cross a reference
explanations: Specializes is the weakest arc and stays weaker than everything else, including the referenced asset's own direct opinion of 0.1. The shot's 0.9 on Steel cannot override it.
0.9 would win if PolishedSteel inherited Steel. With specializes, the specialized prim's own opinions always beat opinions on the base.
Specializes arcs authored inside a referenced asset keep working after the asset is referenced.

0.5 is Steel's value inside the asset and is the weakest opinion here. Even if PolishedSteel authored nothing, the shot's 0.9 on Steel would win over it, because the specializes arc is also implied in the referencing layer stack. 0.5 would show only if neither PolishedSteel nor the shot authored roughness.

questions.stem: This is the same bolt asset, but PolishedSteel now uses inherits instead of specializes. What is the composed roughness of /World/Bolt/Looks/PolishedSteel?
options: 1.0, the average of all authored opinions
explanations: USD never averages opinions; the strongest opinion wins.
An inherit authored inside a referenced asset is also applied (implied) in the referencing layer stack. The shot's opinion on Steel is therefore stronger than the asset's own 0.1.
This is the answer with specializes. With inherits, downstream opinions on the inherited class outrank the referenced asset's direct opinions.
0.5 comes from Steel in the asset, but both the shot's 0.9 and the asset's 0.1 are stronger.

questions.stem: Two drones reference the same animation layer; DroneB uses a layer offset. What is DroneB's xformOp:translate at stage time 15?
explanations: Time samples are not extrapolated, and the offset shifts time rather than adding to values.
An offset of 10 moves the animation 10 frames later, so stage time 15 reads the referenced layer at time 5, halfway between the two samples.
This is DroneA at time 15: without an offset, time 15 is past the last sample and the last value is held.
That would correspond to sampling the animation at time 2.5, for example with an extra scale of 2 on the offset.

questions.stem: Fifty crowd agents must play one shared walk-cycle layer, each starting on a different frame, without copying the animation data. Which approaches achieve this? (Select TWO.)
options: Author a different timeCodesPerSecond on each agent prim.
Reference the walk-cycle layer from each agent with its own layer offset on the reference.
Sublayer the walk-cycle layer into the shot's root layer once per agent.
Set startTimeCode metadata on each agent prim.
Drive each agent with value clips whose clip times map stage time to a shifted clip time.
explanations: timeCodesPerSecond is layer/stage metadata, not prim metadata, and it changes the meaning of time codes rather than offsetting playback.
Layer offsets on references retime the referenced layer per arc, so each agent can start at a different frame while sharing one file.
Sublayers do not remap namespace, so every copy would land on the same prim paths; it cannot target individual agents.
startTimeCode is layer metadata describing a playback range; it does not retime anything.
Value clips can retime data through their (stageTime, clipTime) mapping, which also offsets playback per prim without duplicating samples.

questions.stem: A city set brings in hundreds of building assets with dense geometry. Layout artists often open the set just to move things, and they do not want to wait for every building to load. Which arc should bring each building's heavy contents into the set?
options: Payload
Sublayer
Inherit
Specialize
explanations: Payloads are references that can be left unloaded (for example with Usd.Stage.LoadNone, then Load() on demand), which keeps opening the set fast.
A sublayer is always composed, has no load control, and cannot place an asset at a new prim path.
Inherits broadcast opinions from a class prim; they are not a way to bring in or defer external content.
Specializes provides weak base opinions; it does not offer deferred loading.

questions.stem: Which statements about sublayers are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Sublayers are skipped when the stage is opened with Usd.Stage.LoadNone.
A sublayer contributes its whole namespace as-is; it cannot target a prim or remap paths.
A sublayer can be pointed at one specific prim inside the other file.
Opinions in sublayers count as local opinions of the layer stack they belong to.
subLayers supports prepend and append list editing, just like references.
explanations: Load rules apply to payloads. A sublayer can be excluded by muting it, not by load rules.
Sublayering adds a layer to the layer stack; its prims keep their paths. Retargeting content to a new path needs a reference or payload.
That is what references and payloads do (with an optional prim path); subLayers lists whole layers.
The L in LIVERPS covers the root layer and all of its recursive sublayers.
subLayers is a plain ordered list of layers and is not list-edited.

questions.stem: shot.usda has two sublayers, and the first one has a sublayer of its own. What is the composed size of /World/Table?

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./dressing.usda@,
        @./layout.usda@
    ]
)

options: The prim does not exist, because dressing_notes.usda only contains an over
explanations: layout.usda defines the table, but it is the weakest layer in this stack, so its opinion only applies when no stronger layer has one.
Opinions are not added together; the strongest one wins.
An over composes with the def in layout.usda; the prim is defined and gets the over's value.
Sublayers are gathered depth-first: dressing.usda and its own sublayer dressing_notes.usda are both stronger than layout.usda, which comes later in shot.usda's list.

questions.stem: Right now /World/Ball.radius composes to 1 from base.usda. The supervisor wants tweak.usda's radius of 2 to win without deleting base.usda's opinion. Which change achieves this?

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./base.usda@,
        @./tweak.usda@
    ]
)

options: Write `prepend` in front of the tweak.usda entry in subLayers.
Reorder subLayers in shot.usda so tweak.usda is listed before base.usda.
Set the stage's edit target to tweak.usda.
Change `over` to `def` in tweak.usda.
explanations: subLayers is not a list-edited field, so prepend/append do not apply to it.
Earlier entries in subLayers are stronger. Moving tweak.usda first makes its opinion win while base.usda stays untouched.
An edit target only chooses where new edits are written; it does not make that layer stronger.
The specifier does not affect how strong a property opinion is; layer order does.

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./tweak.usda@,
        @./base.usda@
    ]
)

questions.stem: For which needs is a variant set a good way to structure an asset? (Select TWO.)
options: Storing the per-shot animation of every shot in a film inside the character asset.
Letting the modeling and surfacing departments contribute to the same asset at the same time.
Exposing a continuously adjustable wear amount between 0 and 1.
Switching an asset between high, medium and low level-of-detail representations.
A sofa sold in four discrete fabric looks that set dressers choose between.
explanations: That bloats the asset for every consumer; shot animation belongs in shot layers that reference the character.
Only one variant per set is active, so variants cannot combine two departments' work; separate workstream layers can.
A continuous parameter is better as an attribute or primvar; variants are for discrete choices.
LOD switching is a common variant set: one representation is active at a time and the choice can be made per instance or per shot.
A small set of named, mutually exclusive alternatives is the classic use of a variant set.

questions.stem: An artist added the `over "Chair"` block to shot.usda to move the referenced chair to z = 50, but /World/Chair does not move. Why?
options: xformOp:translate only takes effect when xformOpOrder is authored in the same layer.
An over cannot change an attribute that a referenced layer already authors; a def is needed.
The over is authored at /Chair, which is a different path from /World/Chair, so it overrides nothing and only creates an undefined prim.
Opinions in the root layer are weaker than opinions brought in by references.
explanations: xformOpOrder composes like any other attribute; the value from chair.usda would apply.
Overs are exactly how stronger layers override authored values.
Overs apply by path. The referenced chair lives at /World/Chair, so the over must be nested under `over "World"` (or authored inside the World def).
The opposite is true: local opinions in the root layer stack are the strongest.

questions.stem: An internal asset composes dozens of layers through references, sublayers and variants, and some layer and texture paths are identifiers that only the studio's custom resolver understands (for example studio://props/chair). Before it goes to an outside vendor, which steps make it self-contained? (Select TWO.)
options: Flatten the composed stage (UsdStage::Flatten or `usdcat --flatten`) so the vendor receives a single layer instead of the internal layer structure.
Mute all sublayers before saving so their contents are left out.
Rename every prim to strip the studio's naming convention.
Rewrite asset paths that only the studio resolver understands into relative paths and ship the files they point to (for example packaged into a .usdz).
Change every def to over so the vendor's tools can redefine the prims.
explanations: Flattening bakes the composed result into one layer. Note that only the current variant selections survive, and non-layer assets such as textures still have to travel with it.
Muting removes those layers' opinions from the result, losing real asset data.
Prim names do not create external dependencies; renaming only breaks downstream overrides.
The vendor has no access to the custom resolver, so every remaining asset path must resolve with standard, relative paths.
Prims that are only overs are not defined, so they are skipped by default traversal and rendering.

questions.stem: Both crates in yard.usda are instanceable references to crate.usda. Only Crate_01's Box should lose its wear value; Crate_02 must keep it. Which edits in yard.usda achieve this? (Select TWO.)
options: Keep Crate_01 instanceable and author the blocking over on /Yard/Crate_01/Box.
Set instanceable = false on Crate_01, then author `over "Box" { float wear = None }` beneath it.
Edit the generated prototype prim (for example /__Prototype_1) directly.
Set active = false on Crate_01.
Give Crate_01 an extra inherits arc to a class whose Box child blocks wear; Crate_01 then gets its own prototype and stays instanced.
explanations: Opinions on descendants of an instance are ignored, because the descendants come from the shared prototype.
Deinstancing makes Crate_01's descendants editable again, and a value block (None) removes the 0.8 that the reference brings in.
Prototypes are generated by the stage and cannot be authored to.
That removes the whole crate from the stage instead of just the wear value.
Adding an arc on the instance prim changes its instancing key (ad hoc arc refinement), so it gets a new prototype that includes the block.

questions.stem: Layout, animation and lighting artists edit the same shot at the same time. Which layering choices reduce conflicts while keeping the right department in control? (Select TWO.)
options: Order the department sublayers so the department whose decisions should win is listed first.
Give each department its own layer and sublayer all of them into the shot's root layer.
Put each department's work into its own variant of a single variant set on the shot.
Flatten the shot after every save so later edits overwrite earlier ones.
Have every artist save into the shot's root layer so there is only one file to track.
explanations: Sublayer order sets strength; placing, for example, lighting above layout lets lighting's overrides win where they overlap.
Separate files mean artists never write to the same layer, while the shot still composes everyone's work.
Only one variant is active per set, so the departments' work would never compose together.
Flattening destroys the layer separation that makes collaboration manageable.
Concurrent writes to one layer cause conflicts and lost work.

questions.stem: A single large chair.usd holds the chair's geometry, materials and rigging, so modelers and surfacing artists keep overwriting each other's work. Which restructuring best supports parallel workstreams?
options: Split the content into layers per workstream (for example geo.usd and mtl.usd) and have the asset's contents layer compose them, so each team owns its own file.
Convert chair.usd to .usdc so saves are faster and collide less.
Put geometry and materials into two variants of one variant set.
Keep one file and have the teams take turns locking it.
explanations: Modeling workstreams as separate layers in the asset's layer stack lets each team author sparsely in its own file while the asset still composes into one result.
The encoding does not change who writes to the file.
Variants are mutually exclusive, so the geometry and materials could never be seen together.
Locking serializes the work instead of modeling the workstreams; it does not scale.

questions.stem: A riverbed needs about two million pebbles drawn from five pebble models. Only position, orientation and scale vary per pebble, and nobody will select or edit individual pebbles. Which representation fits best?
options: One variant set with two million variants
Two million separate Mesh prims
Two million instanceable prims, each referencing a pebble asset
A UsdGeomPointInstancer with the five models as prototypes and per-instance arrays
explanations: Variants choose between alternatives; they do not create copies.
Unique meshes multiply memory and composition cost with no benefit here.
Scenegraph instancing shares the pebbles' insides, but you would still pay for two million instance prims and their composition.
Point instancing stores each pebble as array entries rather than as a prim, which scales to millions of copies.

questions.stem: A park layout places 300 copies of a few tree assets. Set dressers must be able to pick each tree, change its transform and sometimes switch its season variant, but nobody edits a tree's internal hierarchy. Which approach fits best?
options: Sublayer every tree file into the layout layer
Reference the tree assets on individual prims marked instanceable
One PointInstancer whose prototypes are the trees
Flatten each tree into the layout layer
explanations: Sublayers do not remap namespace, so all copies would land on the same prim paths.
Each tree keeps its own prim for selection, transforms and variant selections, while trees with the same arcs and selections share a prototype for their internals.
Point instances are not prims, so per-tree selection and variant switching are not natural; point instancing pays off at much larger counts.
Flattening copies all the data into the layout and gives up sharing.

questions.stem: set.usda is opened with Usd.Stage.Open("set.usda", Usd.Stage.LoadNone). Which statements are true? (Select TWO.)
options: /Set/Statue exists and still has the translate authored in set.usda.
/Set/Statue reports kind = component, because kind is read from the payload even when unloaded.
LoadNone also skips references, so referenced prims are missing too.
/Set/Statue/Geom exists but is marked inactive.
/Set/Statue/Geom is not on the stage until the payload is loaded.
explanations: The prim and the opinions authored on it in set.usda are composed regardless of load state.
kind is authored inside the payload, so it is not composed while the payload is unloaded; this is why important metadata is often lofted above the payload.
Load rules only govern payloads; references are always composed.
Unloaded payload contents are absent, which is different from inactive prims.
Everything that comes only from the payload is left out while it is unloaded.

questions.stem: Which list orders the composition arcs from strongest to weakest according to LIVERPS?
options: Local, Inherits, VariantSets, References, Payloads, Specializes, Relocates
Local, References, Inherits, VariantSets, Payloads, Relocates, Specializes
Specializes, Payloads, References, Relocates, VariantSets, Inherits, Local
Local, Inherits, VariantSets, Relocates, References, Payloads, Specializes
explanations: Relocates is not the weakest arc; it comes right after variant sets.
References are weaker than inherits and variant sets.
This is the right sequence read from weakest to strongest, the reverse of what was asked.
This is the LIVERPS order; relocates (the E) sits between variant sets and references.

questions.stem: In shot.usda the Bulb prim both references bulb.usda and selects the "large" variant of a variant set authored in the same layer. What is the composed radius?
explanations: Opinions are not added together.
Variant set opinions (V) are stronger than reference opinions (R), so the selected large variant wins over the asset's 1.
The referenced asset authors 1, but references are weaker than variant sets on the same prim.
0.5 belongs to the unselected small variant; unselected variants contribute nothing.

questions.stem: A script runs `stage = Usd.Stage.Open("shot.usda")`, `stage.SetEditTarget(Usd.EditTarget(Sdf.Layer.FindOrOpen("anim.usda")))`, then `ball.GetAttribute("radius").Set(3.0)` and `print(ball.GetAttribute("radius").Get())`, where ball is the /World/Ball prim. The layers show the files after the script ran. What is printed?
options: 3.0, because the most recent write always wins
Nothing; an error is raised because only the root layer can be an edit target
2.0, because the edit went into anim.usda while shot.usda, the root layer, holds a stronger opinion
3.0, because setting an edit target makes that layer the strongest
explanations: Composition is ordered by layer strength, not by when values were written.
Any layer in the stage's layer stack (here a sublayer) can be the edit target.
The edit target controls where an opinion is written, not how strong it is. The root layer's 2.0 still wins over the sublayer.
Edit targets never change strength ordering.

questions.stem: A script runs `vset = prim.GetVariantSets().AddVariantSet("finish")`, adds the variants "matte" and "gloss", calls `vset.SetVariantSelection("gloss")`, and then needs `prim.GetAttribute("roughness").Set(0.05)` to be stored inside the gloss variant instead of as a direct opinion. What should wrap the Set call?
options: vset.ClearVariantSelection()
with vset.GetVariantEditContext():
stage.SetEditTarget(stage.GetRootLayer())
prim.SetActive(False)
explanations: Clearing the selection only removes the authored choice; it does not redirect edits.
GetVariantEditContext returns an edit context that targets the currently selected variant, so edits made inside the with-block are written into that variant.
That is the default target; the value would still be written as a direct opinion in the root layer.
Deactivating the prim has nothing to do with where edits are authored.

questions.stem: shelf.usda is opened as the root layer. Which statements about this stage are true? (Select TWO.)
options: Calling Set() on torque of /Shelf/Bolt_A/Head writes a new opinion into the current edit target that affects Bolt_A only.
stage.Traverse() visits /Shelf, /Shelf/Bolt_A and /Shelf/Bolt_B, but not the Head prims below them.
stage.GetPrimAtPath("/Shelf/Bolt_A/Head") returns an invalid prim; Head can only be read through the prototype.
Each bolt gets a private copy of Head, so the two Head prims are composed independently.
stage.GetPrimAtPath("/Shelf/Bolt_A/Head").GetPrimInPrototype() and the same call on /Shelf/Bolt_B/Head return the same prim: the Head inside the one shared prototype.
explanations: Authoring to an instance proxy is refused with an error. A change has to go on the instance prim, into the asset, through a broadcast class, or onto a de-instanced copy.
The default traversal predicate stops at instance prims and does not descend into their instance proxies.
GetPrimAtPath returns a valid instance proxy for a path below an instance, so its attributes (torque = 4 here) can be read directly.
Both bolts compose the same arcs, so they share one prototype; the Head prims are proxies onto that shared subtree.
Instance proxies are read-only views onto one prototype subtree; GetPrimInPrototype() maps each proxy to that shared prim (here /__Prototype_1/Head, a generated name that code should not hard-code).

questions.stem: Which statements correctly contrast UsdGeomPointInstancer instances with scenegraph (instanceable) instances? (Select TWO.)
options: A single point instance is not a prim: it has no scene path of its own and is addressed as an index into the instancer's arrays.
Scenegraph instancing only applies to prims whose kind is component; prims of other kinds are silently left uninstanced.
Scenegraph instances cannot carry any per-instance data, because every opinion on the instance prim is discarded.
One point instance can be hidden by listing its id in the instancer's invisibleIds attribute, without touching the prototype or the other instances.
PointInstancer prototypes must live in external files; prototype prims authored beneath the instancer are ignored.
explanations: Point instancing trades addressability for scale: each instance is a row in arrays such as protoIndices and positions, not a prim.
The instanceable flag works on any prim that has composition arcs; kind is a model-hierarchy label and neither enables nor disables instancing.
Opinions on the instance prim itself (transform, visibility, variant selections, constant primvars) are honored; only opinions on its descendants are ignored.
invisibleIds is an int64[] attribute (it can even be time-sampled), so single instances can be hidden without editing prototypes.
Prototypes are usually prims under the instancer, targeted by its prototypes relationship; they may use references, but nothing requires external files.

questions.stem: shot.usda brings props.usda in twice: once as a sublayer and once as a reference on /World/Dressing. Which prims does stage.Traverse() visit?
options: /World, /World/Dressing, /World/Dressing/Crate
/World, /World/Dressing, /World/Dressing/Props, /World/Dressing/Props/Crate
/Props, /Props/Crate, /World, /World/Dressing
/Props, /Props/Crate, /World, /World/Dressing, /World/Dressing/Crate
explanations: This leaves out the sublayer. A sublayer contributes its prims at their own paths, so /Props and /Props/Crate appear as well.
A reference maps its target prim (here the defaultPrim, Props) onto the referencing prim, so Props' children land directly under /World/Dressing with no extra Props level.
The reference does bring Props' child Crate in, remapped to /World/Dressing/Crate.
The sublayer merges props.usda's namespace unchanged (/Props/...), while the reference remaps Props onto /World/Dressing, so Crate shows up in both places.

questions.stem: root.usda holds nothing but a subLayers entry for sub.usda. With root.usda as the root layer, what do UsdGeom.GetStageUpAxis, UsdGeom.GetStageMetersPerUnit, stage.GetStartTimeCode and stage.GetEndTimeCode return?
options: Y, 0.01, 0 and 0: stage-level metadata is read from the root (and session) layer, so sub.usda's values are ignored and the fallbacks apply
Z, 1, 1 and 48: a sublayer contributes its layer metadata just as it contributes its prims
Z and 1, but 0 and 0: geometry metrics come from the first sublayer, while the time code range comes only from the root layer
Nothing: opening fails, because a root layer must author upAxis and metersPerUnit itself
explanations: Layer metadata such as upAxis, metersPerUnit and the time code range counts only on the stage's root (or session) layer. Opening sub.usda directly would report Z, 1, 1 and 48.
Sublayers contribute prim and property opinions, not their stage-level metadata.
UsdGeom reads upAxis and metersPerUnit from stage metadata, which also comes from the root layer; there is no exception for sublayers.
Both values are optional. When they are not authored, UsdGeom returns its fallbacks (Y and 0.01, i.e. centimeters, by default).

scenarios.note: sub.usda opened as the root layer

questions.stem: Which pairings of composition arc and production need are appropriate? (Select THREE.)
options: Sublayer: renaming an asset's root prim from /Lamp to /Lamp_01 as it is brought into a set
Sublayer: stacking the lighting department's opinions over a shot's layout layer, where both describe the same /World hierarchy
Reference: keeping a dense crowd out of memory until a render job asks for it
Reference: placing the same lamp asset ten times under different prim paths in a set
Payload: letting layout artists open a large city set while the heavy building contents stay unloaded
Payload: making sure a department's overrides are present even when the stage is opened with Usd.Stage.LoadNone
explanations: Sublayers merge namespaces unchanged and cannot move a prim to a new path; putting an asset under another name needs a reference.
Sublayers combine layers that describe the same namespace into one layer stack, with the stronger department listed first.
References always compose. Deferring heavy content until it is requested is what payloads (with load rules) are for.
Each reference maps the asset's root prim onto a new prim path, so one asset file can be reused many times.
Payloads can be left unloaded (for example with Usd.Stage.LoadNone or a load rule), so the set opens quickly while the prims that carry the payloads are still there.
Content behind an unloaded payload is absent, so a payload is the wrong arc for opinions that must always apply; use a sublayer or a reference.

questions.stem: /World/Slow references bounce.usda with a layer offset whose scale is 2. What does /World/Slow.height return at stage time 10?
explanations: 25 would be the value at layer time 2.5; at scale 2, stage time 10 reads layer time 5.
With scale 2, layer time t appears at stage time offset + 2t, so stage time 10 reads layer time 5, halfway between 0 and 100.
100 is what /World/Normal (no offset) returns at stage time 10; the scale stretches Slow's clip so it only reaches 100 at stage time 20.
A layer offset stretches time, not values; sampled values are never multiplied by the scale.

questions.stem: ride.usda references bounce.usda with offset 5, and shot.usda references ride.usda with offset 10. At what stage time does /World/Rider.height first reach 100?
options: 10: neither offset applies, because referenced time samples always play at their authored times
15: only the offset nearest to the animation applies
20: only the offset on the outermost reference applies
25: the two offsets accumulate to 15
5: the outer offset is subtracted from the inner one (5 - 10 = -5)
explanations: Both offsets apply: each reference's offset retimes everything brought in through it, including arcs nested inside the referenced layer.
The inner offset alone would put the last sample at stage time 15, but the outer offset adds another 10.
The outer offset alone would give 20; the inner offset of 5 applies as well.
Offsets concatenate along the chain of arcs: layer time 10 lands at 10 + 5 + 10 = 25 on the stage, where the clip reaches 100.
Plain offsets combine by addition when the mappings are chained, not by subtraction.

questions.stem: Both doors reference door.usda; Door_B's reference carries offset = 48. What does /Hall/Door_B.angle return at stage time 12?
options: -135: the first two samples are extrapolated backwards
45: before Door_B's first sample, the default value applies
0: before its first (shifted) sample at stage time 48, the first sample's value is held
No value: Door_B has no animation until stage time 48
explanations: USD does not extrapolate time samples; outside the sampled range it holds the nearest sample.
When the strongest layer has time samples, they win over that layer's default at every time code; the default only answers queries made at the default time code.
offset = 48 moves layer time 0 to stage time 48. Stage time 12 is layer time -36, before the first sample, so its value 0 is held.
Time-sampled attributes return a value at any time: before the first sample the first value is held, after the last the last value is held.

questions.stem: flight.usda was authored at 48 time codes per second; shot.usda runs at 24 and references it with offset = 6. What does /World/Drone.height return at stage time 18?
options: 25: only the offset applies and time codes pass through one-to-one, so stage time 18 reads layer time 12
50: the offset is counted in shot.usda's time codes and the 48/24 rescale applies to flight.usda's codes, so stage time 18 reads layer time (18 - 6) x 2 = 24
75: only the rate conversion applies and the offset is ignored, so stage time 18 reads layer time 36
62.5: the offset is counted in flight.usda's 48-per-second codes, so stage time 18 reads layer time 18 x 2 - 6 = 30
explanations: The two layers declare different timeCodesPerSecond, so composition also rescales time: the 12 shot codes after the offset are half a second, which is code 24 in flight.usda.

The reference's offset is in shot.usda's codes, and the 48/24 rate scale is folded into the same mapping (offset 6, scale 0.5). Stage time t reads layer time (t - 6) x 2, so 18 reads 24, halfway between 0 and 100. The clip reaches 100 at stage time 30.
This ignores the authored offset, which still moves the clip 6 shot codes later.
A reference's offset is expressed in the referencing layer's time codes, not in the referenced layer's.

questions.stem: anim.usda is the stronger sublayer and authors size = 4 on /World/Crate, but stage.Traverse() never reaches the crate. Why?

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./anim.usda@,
        @./layout.usda@
    ]
)

options: anim.usda uses over rather than def, and an over in a stronger layer hides a def from a weaker one.
Sublayers are listed weakest first, so layout.usda is really the stronger layer.
layout.usda sets active = false on the crate and anim.usda authors no active opinion of its own, so the weaker layer's deactivation still decides.
A prim that two departments both author is disabled until one of them removes its opinion.
explanations: Specifiers compose: an over in a stronger layer simply adds opinions on top of the def from the weaker layer.
In subLayers the first entry is the strongest, so anim.usda is stronger than layout.usda.

active is metadata that resolves like any other opinion. Only layout.usda authors it, so the crate stays inactive; size = 4 still composes, but traversal skips inactive prims. Authoring active = true in anim.usda brings the crate back.
USD has no such conflict rule; opinions from several layers simply resolve by strength.

questions.stem: The animators' Car translate in anim.usda is being ignored. Which changes let animation's (5, 0, 0) win while the lamp keeps lighting's intensity of 10? (Select TWO.)

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./lighting.usda@,
        @./anim.usda@,
        @./layout.usda@
    ]
)

options: Set the stage's edit target to anim.usda before the shot is opened.
Delete the stray Car translate from lighting.usda.
Move layout.usda to the front of shot.usda's subLayers.
Change anim.usda's over "Car" to def "Car".
List anim.usda before lighting.usda in shot.usda's subLayers.
explanations: An edit target only decides where new edits are written; it never changes how existing opinions resolve.
With the stray opinion gone, anim.usda is the strongest layer that authors the Car translate, and lighting.usda still owns the lamp.
layout.usda would then win everything it authors, including intensity = 1 on the lamp and (0, 0, 0) on the car.
def and over do not change strength; the stronger lighting.usda would still win.
anim.usda becomes stronger than lighting.usda. It authors nothing on the lamp, so lighting's intensity of 10 still wins there.

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./anim.usda@,
        @./lighting.usda@,
        @./layout.usda@
    ]
)

#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./layout.usda@,
        @./lighting.usda@,
        @./anim.usda@
    ]
)

scenarios.note: def instead of over in anim.usda

questions.stem: A lighter wants to hide a few heavy set pieces only for today's interactive session. Nothing may be saved into the department layers or the shot's root layer. Where should the visibility edits be authored?
options: In the stage's session layer, by setting the edit target to stage.GetSessionLayer()
In the weakest department sublayer, so that other departments can easily override them
In a new sublayer appended to the end of the shot's subLayers
Directly in the referenced asset files, since visibility belongs to the asset
explanations: The session layer sits above the root layer, so its opinions win, and stage.Save() does not save it; the tweaks vanish with the session unless someone exports them.
That writes into a saved department file, and as the weakest layer its opinions could be overridden by stronger departments anyway.
An appended sublayer is the weakest layer, and it becomes a permanent part of the shot once the root layer is saved.
Editing the assets changes every shot that uses them, the opposite of a temporary local tweak.

questions.stem: shot.usda authors relocates layer metadata for the Arm prim that rig.usda brings in through a reference. What does the composed stage contain?
options: /World/Rig/Arm with length 2, plus an unrelated, empty /World/Rig/LeftArm created by the over
Both /World/Rig/Arm and /World/Rig/LeftArm, each with length 2
/World/Rig/LeftArm with length 2, because relocates are weaker than the reference that brought Arm in
/World/Rig/LeftArm with length 3, and no prim at /World/Rig/Arm
explanations: Relocates move the referenced prim to the new path, so the over at LeftArm lands on the moved prim instead of creating a separate one.
A relocation is a move, not a copy: the source path no longer exists on the stage.
The over at the new path is a local opinion in the root layer stack, so it beats the referenced asset's opinion; the relocation only changes where the asset's opinions land.
The relocates entry moves the referenced Arm to LeftArm; local opinions are then authored at the new path, so length 3 wins over the asset's 2.

questions.stem: In tree.usda, Tree inherits </_Foliage>. forest.usda references tree.usda on /Forest/Oak and also authors a class at /_Foliage. What is /Forest/Oak.leafDensity?
options: 0.5: the inherits arc lives inside tree.usda, so only tree.usda's class can affect it
1.4: the two class opinions are added together
0.9: the inherit targets a path outside the referenced prim, so it also resolves /_Foliage on the referencing stage, where forest.usda's opinion is stronger
No value: /_Foliage lies outside the referenced prim, so the inherit has nothing to read
explanations: An inherit that targets a path outside the referenced prim is global: the referencing layer stack can author the same class path, and its opinions win.
Attribute values never accumulate across arcs; value resolution picks one strongest opinion.
The inherit maps to /_Foliage on the referencing stage. forest.usda's class opinion sits in the root layer stack and beats the class inside the reference; remove it and the value falls back to 0.5.
Composition still follows the inherit into tree.usda's own /_Foliage even though that prim is not brought onto the stage; without forest.usda's class the value would be 0.5.

questions.stem: An asset librarian is reviewing requests to add variant sets to library assets. Which two requests should be turned down because a variant set cannot express the need well? (Select TWO.)
options: A traffic light that must switch from red to green at frame 120 of a shot
A street sign asset that shows one of six discrete faces, chosen per placement
A building that layout shows either intact or damaged, decided per shot
A vehicle offered as sedan, coupe or convertible body styles
Giving each of 5,000 rocks its own random rotation and scale
explanations: A variant selection is metadata, not an attribute, so it cannot be time-sampled; a change over time needs animated attributes instead.
A small fixed set of mutually exclusive looks picked per placement is a classic fit for a variant set.
Discrete per-shot states fit well: the shot authors the selection without touching the asset.
Discrete product configurations fit a variant set well.
Continuous per-copy values do not map to a discrete list of variants; author them as attributes on each copy, or as per-instance arrays on a PointInstancer.

questions.stem: room.usda selects the size variant "Large" on the referenced lamp. What does /Room/Lamp.bulbRadius return?
options: 5: variant names are matched without regard to case
No value: the selection names a variant that does not exist, so no size variant contributes, and the stronger selection still overrides the asset's default of small
2: when a selection names no existing variant, the asset's own default selection is used instead
Nothing composes: the stage reports a composition error and the lamp is empty
explanations: Variant names are case-sensitive; "Large" and "large" are different names.
bulbRadius exists only inside the variants, so with no matching variant the attribute is not defined at all. Changing the selection to "large" gives 5.
The selection in room.usda is stronger than the asset's own, even when it names a missing variant; there is no fallback to the weaker selection.
Selecting a missing variant is not a composition error; the variant set simply contributes nothing.

questions.stem: Each lod variant in tree.usda defines Geom with a reference to a different geometry file. tree.usda is opened as the root layer. Which statements are true? (Select TWO.)
options: Both geometry files are always composed; the variant only toggles which one is visible.
References cannot be authored inside a variant, so Geom stays empty.
With the authored selection, /Tree/Geom has exactly one child, Card.
Selecting high keeps Card and adds Trunk and Leaves, because variant contents are merged.
Selecting high gives /Tree/Geom the children Trunk and Leaves instead, because only the selected variant's reference is composed.
explanations: Arcs inside an unselected variant are not composed at all, so the other geometry file is not even opened.
Variants may hold any scene description, including references and payloads; swapping representations this way is common.
low is selected, so only tree_low.usda is referenced and Geom gets its Card child.
Only one variant of a set is selected at a time; the low variant's reference disappears when high is selected.
With high selected, Geom's reference points at tree_high.usda, giving Trunk and Leaves and no Card.

questions.stem: strong.usda keys /World/Ball.radius, and the weaker weak.usda authors radius = 7. What do radius.Get() (no time argument) and radius.Get(12) return?

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./strong.usda@,
        @./weak.usda@
    ]
)

options: 0 and 12: at the default time, the strongest layer's first time sample is returned
7 and 7: a weaker layer's default always beats time samples
7 and 12: a default-time query consults only default values, so it falls through to weak.usda's default, while Get(12) resolves strong.usda's samples
None and 12: a default-time query returns nothing when the strongest opinion is time-sampled
explanations: Get() with no time asks for Usd.TimeCode.Default(), which never reads time samples.
At time 12 strength decides: strong.usda's samples are the strongest opinion and interpolate to 12, so weak.usda's default is never reached.

At the default time a layer that holds only samples gives no answer, so resolution moves on to weak.usda's default of 7. At a numeric time strong.usda's samples win, and 12 lies on the line from 0 to 24.
The query falls through to weaker defaults, or to the schema fallback (1 for Sphere.radius) when none is authored; here weak.usda supplies 7.

questions.stem: A lighter set the night intensity in base.usda to 2, and base.usda selects night, yet /World/Sun.intensity reads 1000. Why?

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./look.usda@,
        @./base.usda@
    ]
)

options: Only the first variant authored in a set can be selected from a sublayer.
Variant opinions are weaker than any default value, so 1000 is the attribute's fallback.
Variant selections may only be authored in the root layer, so base.usda's selection is ignored.
look.usda is the stronger sublayer and selects day; a variant selection is an opinion like any other, so the stronger one decides which variant contributes.
explanations: Any variant can be selected from any layer; its position in the set does not matter.
1000 is not a fallback; it is the value authored inside the day variant.
Selections can be authored in any layer and resolve by strength like other metadata.
The edit to the night variant is correct but unused while day is selected. Removing look.usda's selection (or selecting night there) gives 2.

questions.stem: room.usda is flattened with stage.Flatten(), and only the flattened layer is sent to a vendor. Which statements describe the vendor's stage? (Select TWO.)
options: spin reads 5 at time 10, just as on the original stage, because the offset was baked into the sample times.
spin still has samples at times 0 and 10, so the vendor must re-apply the 5-frame offset.
The flattened layer still references chair.usda, so the vendor needs that file as well.
/Room/Chair can no longer switch to walnut: only the opinions of the selected oak variant were written out, not the variant set.
vendorCode is gone, because flattening drops opinions that came from inherited classes.
explanations: Flattening bakes layer offsets into the written sample times (here 5 and 15), so the timing is preserved.
The offset is already applied to the written samples; applying it again would shift the animation twice.
Flattening resolves every arc into plain prim specs, so the result does not reference chair.usda.
Flatten writes the composed result for the current selection; the variant set and the walnut opinions are not part of it.
Inherited opinions are baked in like any other, so vendorCode = "internal" is still there and has to be stripped by hand if it is studio-only.

questions.stem: A TD flattens an internal asset before sending it to an outside partner. Which follow-up checks are still needed? (Select THREE.)
options: Re-author every layer offset, since flattening throws offsets away and changes the animation timing.
Strip studio-only metadata such as internal customData or assetInfo identifiers, because flattening copies prim metadata through.
Clear or rewrite the flattened layer's doc metadata: stage.Flatten() records "Generated from Composed Stage of root layer" followed by the absolute path of the TD's root layer.
Rebuild the variant sets, or the flattened layer will fail to open.
Gather the non-layer files the asset needs, such as textures (UsdUtils.ComputeAllDependencies lists them and a .usdz package can carry them), because flattening merges only scene description.
None: a flattened layer is guaranteed to be self-contained.
explanations: Offsets are baked into the written sample times, so the timing is already right.
Flatten keeps metadata such as customData and assetInfo, including internal identifiers a partner should not see.
Flatten writes that doc string into the result's layer metadata, so an internal file path travels with the delivery unless it is cleared (for example flattened.documentation = "") or rewritten.
A flattened layer opens fine without variant sets; it simply holds only the selected variant's opinions.
Textures and other non-layer assets are not embedded in a .usda layer; they have to be collected and shipped, for example inside a .usdz package.
Flattening only resolves composition; metadata, asset paths and external files still need attention.

questions.stem: A partner wants a shot delivered as a single layer but must still be able to switch the variants of the assets in it; the referenced asset files travel in the same package. Which approach fits?
options: UsdUtils.FlattenLayerStack(stage) (or usdcat --flattenLayerStack), which merges only the root layer stack's sublayers into one layer and keeps references, payloads and variant sets as live arcs
stage.Flatten(), followed by re-creating the variant sets by hand in the result
rootLayer.Export(), which writes the root layer with every sublayer and reference baked in
usdcat on the root layer with no options, which flattens all composition arcs
explanations: Flattening only the layer stack collapses the sublayers into one file while leaving the arcs, and therefore the variant sets, live for the partner. By default it rewrites relative asset paths, including the reference paths, as absolute paths anchored to the source layers, so make them relative again before packaging.
Stage-level flattening discards the unselected variants, and rebuilding them by hand is slow and error-prone.
SdfLayer.Export writes just that layer's own content; its sublayers and references stay external.
Without --flatten or --flattenLayerStack, usdcat only rewrites the layer (for example to another format); it does not flatten anything.

questions.stem: room.usda's two chairs are instanceable references to chair.usda. The stage is flattened and the result is opened on its own. What happens to the instancing?
options: It is lost: each chair is written out as a full, separate copy of its hierarchy.
It is kept: the flattened layer holds one shared prototype prim that both chairs reference internally, so they still compose as instances of one prototype.
instanceable = true is kept, but the chairs still reference chair.usda as an external file.
Flattening refuses to run on a stage with instances; the chairs must be de-instanced first.
explanations: Flatten preserves scenegraph instancing instead of expanding every instance.
Flatten writes each prototype once as a root prim and points the instance prims at it with an internal reference, keeping instanceable = true.
No external arcs remain after flattening; the prototype's content is written into the flattened layer itself.
Instanced stages flatten without any special preparation.

questions.stem: Lamp_02 in street.usda authors two value blocks. Which statements are true? (Select TWO.)
options: Lamp_02.debugTag has no value: debugTag lives on the instance prim itself, and opinions on an instance prim are honored.
Lamp_02/Bulb.flicker is blocked, because value blocks are allowed below instances.
Blocking debugTag forces Lamp_02 into a prototype of its own.
Both blocks are ignored, because nothing at all can be authored on an instanceable prim.
Lamp_02/Bulb.flicker still reads 0.3, because opinions on descendants of an instance are ignored.
explanations: The instance prim is an ordinary, editable prim; only what sits below it comes from the shared prototype.
The over on Bulb targets an instance proxy path, which composition ignores; changing it needs a class, a variant, the asset itself or de-instancing.
Properties authored on the instance prim do not take part in prototype sharing; both lamps still share one prototype.
The instance prim itself accepts opinions; only its descendants do not.
Bulb is an instance proxy of the shared prototype, so the local over is discarded and the asset's 0.3 stays.

questions.stem: Lamp_01 selects the flicker variant "off" on its instance prim. What is the result?
options: The selection is ignored on an instanceable prim, so all three lamps read 0.3 and share one prototype.
All three lamps lose flicker, because instances always share a single prototype.
Lamp_01/Bulb.flicker has no value, Lamp_02 and Lamp_03 keep 0.3, and the stage now has two prototypes.
Lamp_01/Bulb.flicker has no value, and Lamp_01 is no longer an instance.
explanations: Variant selections on the instance prim are honored; they are one of the supported ways to vary instances.
Instances share a prototype only when their arcs and selections match, and Lamp_01's selection differs.
The off selection composes a different hierarchy, so Lamp_01 gets its own prototype while Lamp_02 and Lamp_03 keep sharing the on prototype, all without de-instancing.
Lamp_01 stays instanceable; it just uses a different prototype.

questions.stem: A chair was split into geo.usda (modeling) and mtl.usda (surfacing), combined by contents.usda. Modeling left a placeholder binding behind. Which material is /Chair/Seat bound to?
options: /Chair/Looks/Grey: the layer that defines the prims with def always wins over layers that only use over
/Chair/Looks/Oak: mtl.usda is listed first in subLayers, so it is the stronger layer
Both: material:binding targets from all layers are merged
None: Oak is a def nested under over prims in mtl.usda, so it never becomes a real prim
explanations: def and over do not affect strength; the order of subLayers does.
The first sublayer is the strongest, and its explicitly authored target replaces the weaker one. Listing geo.usda first would bind Grey instead.
An explicit target list in a stronger layer replaces weaker lists; only prepend/append list edits would combine.
On the composed stage geo.usda supplies the def for Chair and Looks, so Oak is a defined prim.

questions.stem: A monolithic prop is split into geo.usda, mtl.usda and rig.usda, sublayered into one contents layer that the asset's entry layer brings in. Which benefits does this give? (Select TWO.)
options: Each workstream may use its own root prim name, since sublayers remap namespaces.
The asset's entry layer no longer needs a defaultPrim.
Modeling, surfacing and rigging can save their own files at the same time without overwriting each other.
The sublayer order in the contents layer is an explicit, reviewable rule for whose opinion wins when two workstreams author the same property.
Sublayered workstream files load lazily like payloads, so modelers never load rigging data.
explanations: Sublayers never remap namespaces; all workstream layers must describe the same root prim (for example /Chair).
The entry layer still needs a defaultPrim so the asset can be referenced without a prim path.
Separate files mean separate saves, locks and version history for each workstream.
Strength follows the subLayers order, so conflicts resolve predictably and can be changed by reordering.
Sublayers are always composed; deferred loading needs a payload (for example from the entry layer to the contents layer).

questions.stem: To make radius 9 win, a TD put it inside a variant in fix.usda, the strongest sublayer, yet /World/Ball.radius still reads 1. Which single edit makes 9 win?

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./fix.usda@,
        @./base.usda@
    ]
)

options: Move fix.usda after base.usda in subLayers.
Change over "Ball" to def "Ball" in fix.usda.
Add a matching size variant set to base.usda and select big there too.
Author radius = 9 directly on /World/Ball in fix.usda, outside the variant set.
explanations: That makes fix.usda weaker still, and base.usda's direct opinion keeps winning.
The specifier does not change strength; the variant opinion is still outranked.
base.usda's direct radius = 1 would still be a local opinion, and local opinions outrank every variant opinion in the layer stack.
Direct (local) opinions anywhere in the root layer stack beat variant opinions, even when the variant sits in a stronger sublayer; a direct opinion in the strongest sublayer wins.

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./base.usda@,
        @./fix.usda@
    ]
)

questions.stem: fix.usda, the stronger sublayer, adds b.usda to /World/Thing's references, but weight still reads 1. Which edit to fix.usda makes weight read 2 while keeping what a.usda contributes (such as supplier)?

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./fix.usda@,
        @./base.usda@
    ]
)

options: Change append references to prepend references.
Replace it with an explicit list: references = @./b.usda@.
Change it to delete references = @./a.usda@.
Nothing needs to change: references added by a stronger layer always outrank references from weaker layers.
explanations: List edits from all layers combine into one ordered list in which earlier entries are stronger. Prepending puts b.usda ahead of a.usda, and supplier still comes from a.usda.
An explicit list in the stronger layer replaces the weaker list entirely, so a.usda (and supplier) would be dropped.
Swapping the append for a delete of a.usda leaves Thing with no references at all, so weight and supplier both disappear.
Appended items go to the end of the combined list, so b.usda stays weaker than a.usda no matter which layer appended it.

scenarios.note: delete a.usda instead of appending b.usda

questions.stem: The third instance of /Forest/Rocks must become a Slab instead of a Boulder. The Slab prim already exists under Prototypes. Which edit is correct?
options: Add </Forest/Rocks/Prototypes/Slab> as the second target of prototypes and set protoIndices to [0, 0, 1].
Only set protoIndices to [0, 0, 1]; the Slab is picked up because it lives under the instancer.
Add the Slab to prototypes and append a fourth position, leaving protoIndices with three entries.
Set protoIndices to [0, 0, "Slab"] so the third instance picks the prototype by name.
explanations: protoIndices index into the ordered targets of the prototypes relationship, so the new prototype must be targeted before an instance can use index 1.
Being a descendant is not enough; with a single prototype target, index 1 is out of range.
That adds an instance instead of changing one, and leaves the per-instance arrays with mismatched lengths.
protoIndices is an int[] attribute; prototypes are chosen by index, never by name.

questions.stem: You need 40 specific instances of a 100,000-instance PointInstancer to stop rendering, without rewriting its per-instance arrays. Which mechanisms are designed for this? (Select TWO.)
options: Set visibility = invisible on the prototype prims.
Prune them through the inactiveIds list-op metadata (for example with PointInstancer.DeactivateIds).
Move those instances into a second PointInstancer and deactivate it.
List their ids in the invisibleIds attribute (for example with PointInstancer.InvisIds(ids, time)).
Delete their entries from positions and leave the other arrays unchanged.
explanations: That hides every instance that uses those prototypes, not just the 40 chosen ones.
inactiveIds deactivates instances entirely; it cannot vary over time but can be list-edited sparsely in stronger layers.
This rewrites the arrays of both instancers, which is exactly what was to be avoided.

invisibleIds hides instances and can be time-sampled, which suits instances that blink on and off. Do not confuse this with MakeInvisible(), which is inherited from UsdGeomImageable and sets visibility = invisible on the whole PointInstancer prim.
That rewrites the data and leaves protoIndices, orientations and scales out of sync with positions.

questions.stem: Lamp_01 and Lamp_02 are instances of the same lamp asset. room.usda authors a displayColor primvar on the Lamp_01 instance prim itself. What is the result?
options: Lamp_02 also turns red, because both lamps share a prototype.
Nothing changes, because no opinion can be authored on an instanceable prim.
Lamp_01 is automatically deinstanced so the color can be applied.
Lamp_01's Shade mesh inherits the red primvar from its instance prim, and Lamp_01 stays an instance sharing a prototype with Lamp_02.
explanations: The primvar lives on Lamp_01, outside the prototype, so only Lamp_01's subtree inherits it.
Only the descendants of an instance are locked; the instance prim itself can carry overrides such as transforms and primvars.
USD never deinstances on its own; instancing only changes when instanceable or the arcs change.

Opinions on the instance prim itself are allowed, and constant primvars are inherited down namespace. Because the mesh does not author its own displayColor, the inherited value applies without breaking instancing.

questions.stem: yard.usda places four crates. A and B are instanceable and both select wear = clean (with different transforms), C is instanceable and selects dirty, and D is not instanceable. How many prototypes does the stage create?
explanations: Instances with identical arcs and selections share prototypes rather than getting one each.
C cannot share with A and B, because its variant selection gives it different composed contents.
A and B share one prototype: same arcs, same variant selection, and transforms on the instance prims do not matter. C needs a second prototype. D is not an instance at all.
D does not create a prototype because it is not instanceable.

questions.stem: A script walks an assembly with Usd.PrimRange(root, Usd.TraverseInstanceProxies()) and calls `prim.GetAttribute("size").Set(2.0)` on a Cube found beneath an instanceable prim. What happens?
options: The value is silently written into the referenced asset's layer.
USD rejects the edit with an error, because authoring to an instance proxy is not allowed.
Only this instance changes, and USD deinstances it automatically.
Every instance that shares the prototype changes, because the value is written into the prototype.
explanations: Edits go to the edit target, and this one is refused before anything is written.
Instance proxies are read-only views of the shared prototype. To change them, edit the instance prim, a broadcast class, an added arc, or deinstance.
USD does not deinstance on its own, and it does not author through instance proxies.
Prototypes are generated by the stage and are never an authoring destination.

questions.stem: Every crate in yard.usda is an instanceable reference to crate.usda, whose root prim inherits </_class_Crate>. yard.usda authors the class shown. What is the result for both crates?
options: wear is blocked (no value) on every crate's Box, and the crates stay instances that share one prototype.
wear is blocked, but instancing is switched off for every crate.
Only Crate_01 is affected, because a class applies to the first instance only.
wear still reads 0.8, because class opinions never reach the descendants of instances.
explanations: The asset's inherit arc is implied in the yard's layer stack, so the class opinion is broadcast to every crate, and all of them still share the same, refined prototype.
Nothing changes instanceable; the crates' composition stays identical, so they keep sharing a prototype.
A class applies to every prim that inherits it.
Broadcasting through inherits (or specializes) is one of the supported ways to refine instances.

questions.stem: Given city.usda, which of the listed prims does UsdPrim.IsModel() report as models? (Select TWO.)
options: /City/Block_A/Kiosk/Sign
/City/Loose/Bench
/City/Block_A/Kiosk
/City/Block_A
explanations: subcomponent is not a model kind; it marks an important prim inside a component.
Its parent Loose has no kind, which breaks the model hierarchy, so Bench is not a model even though it says component.
A component whose ancestors are all groups or assemblies is a model.
group is a model kind, and its parent /City is an assembly (a kind of group), so the model hierarchy is intact.

questions.stem: A stadium assembly contains 80 identical seating sections, and each section asset contains 500 identical seats. Which statement about instancing this content is correct?
options: The sections can be instanceable, and the seats inside the section asset can be instanceable too; prototypes may themselves contain instances.
USD forbids instanceable prims inside a prototype, so only one level can be instanced.
The sections must be flattened before their seats can be instanced.
Only PointInstancers can be nested; scenegraph instances cannot.
explanations: This is nested instancing. It multiplies the savings, but keep the scheme simple enough to understand and refine.
Nested instancing is supported.
No flattening is required; instancing is driven by instanceable metadata and composition arcs.
Scenegraph instances can be nested inside prototypes.

questions.stem: Which statements about UsdGeomPointInstancer data are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Per-instance arrays such as orientations and scales, when authored, must have the same length as positions.
orientations stores Euler angles in degrees.
Each point instance is its own prim that can be selected by prim path.
A PointInstancer can only have one prototype.
protoIndices stores, per instance, an index into the ordered targets of the prototypes relationship.
explanations: Each array holds one entry per instance, so the lengths have to agree.
orientations holds quaternions (quath[]), not Euler angles.
Point instances are entries in arrays, not prims; that is what makes them cheap.
prototypes is a relationship that can target many prototype prims.
That index chooses which prototype each point instance draws.

questions.stem: room.usda tries to tint the Lamp_01 instance red with a constant displayColor on the instance prim, but Lamp_01 still looks grey. What does FindPrimvarWithInheritance("displayColor") return for /Room/Lamp_01/Shade, and why?
options: (0.9, 0.1, 0.1), because an opinion on the instance prim is stronger than anything inside its prototype.
(0.5, 0.5, 0.5), because the displayColor that Shade authors itself takes precedence over the inherited one.
No value, because composition drops any primvars that are authored on instanceable prims.
(0.9, 0.1, 0.1) on both lamps, because the two instances share a single prototype.
explanations: The instance prim's opinion is honored, but inheritance only supplies a primvar to descendants that have no value of their own.

Inheritance fills a primvar in only where the descendant has no authored value. For per-instance tinting the asset must leave Shade's displayColor unauthored (or block it in the asset) so the value on the instance prim can show through.
The instance prim itself can carry opinions such as primvars and transforms; only its descendants are locked.
The primvar sits on Lamp_01, outside the shared prototype, so it never reaches Lamp_02.

questions.stem: room.usda binds /Room/Looks/Red on the Lamp_01 instance prim, yet ComputeBoundMaterial() for /Room/Lamp_01/Shade still returns the asset's Brass material. Which edit in room.usda makes that shade resolve to Red while Lamp_01 stays an instance sharing its prototype with Lamp_02?
options: Give Lamp_01's material:binding relationship the metadata bindMaterialAs = "strongerThanDescendants".
Add `over "Shade"` beneath Lamp_01 with its own material:binding to </Room/Looks/Red>.
Set instanceable = false on Lamp_01 and bind Red directly on /Room/Lamp_01/Shade.
Define a copy of the Red material as a child of /Room/Lamp_01 so that it becomes part of the instance.
explanations: By default a prim's own binding beats an ancestor's binding. strongerThanDescendants on the ancestor's binding reverses that, and because the opinion sits on the instance prim, the prototype is untouched.
Shade is an instance proxy, and opinions authored beneath an instance are ignored.
It would look right, but it deinstances Lamp_01, which the requirement rules out.
An instance's children come only from its prototype, so a child defined locally under the instance is ignored.

questions.stem: Both lamps are instances of lamp.usda, whose material reads a tint primvar that the asset exposes on its root prim. Lamp_02 must turn green while still sharing one prototype with Lamp_01. Which edit in room.usda does that?
options: Author the same green, constant tint primvar on /Room/Lamp_02/Shade, the mesh being shaded.
Override inputs:diffuseColor with green on /Room/Lamp_02/Looks/Tinted/Surface.
Point Lamp_02 at a copy of lamp.usda in which the root prim's tint is already green.
Author a constant `primvars:tint = [(0, 1, 0)]` on /Room/Lamp_02 itself.
explanations: Shade is an instance proxy, so that opinion is ignored.
The shader is inside the instance as well, so this override is ignored; it would also bypass the parameter the asset exposes.
Referencing a different file changes Lamp_02's composition, so it would get a prototype of its own.
Lamp_02 is the instance prim, so its local opinion beats the referenced white tint, and the reader picks up the inherited value. Nothing inside the prototype changes, so both lamps keep sharing it.

scenarios.note: green tint on the Lamp_02 instance prim

questions.stem: Three robot arms share one prototype, and one of them has to look different. Which statements about refining that one instance are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Authoring an over at /__Prototype_1 in a layer is a supported, persistent way to change the shared prototype for every instance.
Instance proxies become editable once the edit target is set to the root layer of the stage.
Opinions on the instanceable prim itself, such as a transform or a constant primvar, keep instancing intact.
Selecting a different variant on one instance can never change which prototype that instance uses.
A constant primvar on the instanceable prim can drive a material inside the prototype.
explanations: /__Prototype_N is a name the stage generates at runtime, and it is not stable between sessions. The Usd API refuses edits on prototype prims. A spec written into a layer at that path with Sdf collides with the generated prototype instead of editing it, and can corrupt the stage (usd-core 26.8 crashes when such a layer is opened). Change shared content in the asset, or through a class it inherits.
Instance proxies are read-only whatever the edit target; authoring through them is an error.
Only the descendants of an instance are locked; the instanceable prim itself is editable.
A different variant selection changes the composed arcs, so that instance moves to a different prototype (it remains an instance).
This is hierarchical refinement with primvars: the prototype stays identical, a shader reads the inherited value, and only that instance looks different.

questions.stem: Which lantern does the invisibleIds value below hide?
options: The lantern at x = 2, the second entry of positions.
Every lantern whose protoIndices value is 1.
None of them, because invisibleIds only works when ids is not authored.
The lantern at x = 4, whose id is 1.
explanations: That would be the answer without an ids array, when instance ids are simply the array indices.
invisibleIds lists instance ids, not prototype indices.
ids exists precisely so that hiding and pruning can name instances by a stable id.
When ids is authored, invisibleIds (and inactiveIds) name instances by their id values, so id 1 is the third entry, at x = 4.

questions.stem: No ids are authored on the Rocks instancer. Which instances are drawn at frame 30 and at frame 60?
options: Frame 30: all four. Frame 60: the instances at indices 0 and 2.
Frame 30: indices 0 and 2, because the hidden set blends toward the frame-50 sample.
Both frames: all four, because invisibleIds cannot be animated.
Frame 30: none of them. Frame 60: the instances at indices 1 and 3.
explanations: Integer arrays are not interpolated: each sample holds until the next one, so the empty list from frame 0 applies at 30 and [1, 3] applies from frame 50 on. Without ids, the listed values are indices.
Id arrays are held between samples, never blended.
invisibleIds is an ordinary attribute and can be time-sampled, which is what makes it the tool for visibility that changes over time.
The listed values are the hidden instances, not the drawn ones, and frame 30 still uses the empty frame-0 sample.

questions.stem: In a PointInstancer of 200,000 rocks, one rock must disappear at frame 100 and come back at frame 140, while every other rock stays as it is. Which approach fits?
options: Prune the rock through inactiveIds, for example with PointInstancer.DeactivateIds([id]) at frame 100.
Time-sample invisibleIds: [] at the first frame, [id] at frame 100 and [] at frame 140.
Author visibility = invisible on the PointInstancer at frame 100 and visible again at frame 140.
Remove the rock's entries from positions and protoIndices in samples covering frames 100 to 139.
explanations: inactiveIds is list-op metadata and cannot change over time (DeactivateIds takes no time), so the rock would be pruned for the whole shot.
invisibleIds is an attribute, so it can be time-sampled. Samples are held, so the empty sample before frame 100 matters: a lone sample at frame 100 would also apply to every earlier frame.
That hides every rock the instancer draws.
Rewriting the per-instance arrays is heavy and changes their lengths between samples; hiding exists so you do not have to.

questions.stem: A set dresser has to hide or prune some rocks in a large PointInstancer without rebuilding it. Which facts about the available mechanisms are right? (Select THREE.)
options: ComputeInstanceTransformsAtTime() skips masked (inactive or invisible) instances by default.
invisibleIds is a relationship that targets the prototype prims whose instances should be hidden.
inactiveIds is list-op metadata, so a stronger layer can add or remove single ids.
invisibleIds may only contain ids that are already listed in the inactiveIds metadata.
visibility = invisible on the PointInstancer prim hides all of its instances at once.
explanations: By default the computation applies the mask from ComputeMaskAtTime(), so inactive and invisible instances drop out; IgnoreMask returns every instance.
invisibleIds is an int64[] attribute of instance ids, which is also why it can be animated.
As a list op it composes like other list-edited data: a stronger layer can prepend, append or delete ids without restating the whole list.
The two are independent: one hides instances, the other prunes them.
Visibility is inherited down namespace, so an invisible PointInstancer hides itself, the prototypes beneath it and every instance it draws.

questions.stem: An assembly layer must make wear disappear from a component whose published asset layer authors it. The assembly layer is stronger, and it is the only file you may edit. What does removing the property amount to in USD?
options: Writing `delete float wear` in the assembly layer, which deletes the asset's spec for that attribute.
Authoring a value block (wear = None) in an opinion that reaches the property; the asset's spec itself stays.
Calling prim.RemoveProperty("wear") with the assembly layer as edit target, which strips the property from every layer.
Changing the attribute's variability to uniform in the assembly layer, which hides it from value resolution.
explanations: No USDA statement deletes a weaker layer's property spec; delete is a list-op operation for lists such as references or relationship targets.

A stronger layer cannot delete a weaker layer's spec, but a block stops value resolution with no value. For instances, the block must reach the prototype (for example through a class the asset inherits) or sit on the instance prim itself.
RemoveProperty only removes the property's spec in the current edit target, so the asset's opinion still composes.
Variability does not hide values.

questions.stem: shot.usda adds a Slab prototype to the rocks by list-editing the prototypes relationship and changes nothing else. What do the three instances draw now?
options: Instance 0 draws Boulder and instances 1 and 2 draw Pebble; Slab stays unused until protoIndices point at it.
Composition fails, because a prototypes relationship cannot be list-edited from another layer.
Instance 0 draws Boulder and instances 1 and 2 draw Slab.
Instance 0 draws Slab and instances 1 and 2 draw Boulder, because prepend shifted every index.
explanations: That is what append would give: it adds the new target at the end of the ordered list.
Relationship targets are list-edited like other list ops.
Indices are positions in the target list; nothing maps index 1 to Slab.

protoIndices index into the composed, ordered target list. prepend puts Slab at index 0, so Boulder moves to 1 and Pebble to 2. Append new prototypes (or rewrite protoIndices) to keep existing instances stable.

questions.stem: A PointInstancer authors only positions, protoIndices and the prototypes relationship. You add a Crate prototype and two new instances that use it. Which edits are required? (Select THREE.)
options: Add a separate Crate prim under the instancer for each of the two new instances.
Add one target for the Crate prototype to the prototypes relationship.
Append two entries to protoIndices, both holding the Crate prototype's index in the target list.
Append two entries to invisibleIds.
Append two entries to positions.
explanations: A prototype is targeted once; instances are entries in the per-instance arrays, not prims.
Each distinct prototype needs exactly one target in prototypes.
protoIndices must stay as long as positions, and the new entries select the new target by its index.
invisibleIds only lists instances to hide; it is not a per-instance array.
Every instance needs a position, so positions grows by two.

questions.stem: The tree prototypes live under an over named Prototypes inside the instancer. Which statements are true? (Select TWO.)
options: A prototype can be an Xform with children; it need not be a single Mesh.
The instancer draws nothing, because its prototypes are not defined prims.
stage.Traverse() skips the prototypes, because a prim under an over is not defined.
Prototypes must be root prims of the stage, so this layout is invalid.
Both trees use the Pine prototype, because protoIndices are counted from 1.
explanations: Prototypes are whole prim hierarchies, as Pine and Oak show.
The instancer reaches its prototypes through the relationship; the over only keeps default traversals away from them, which is the practice Learn OpenUSD recommends.

The default traversal visits only /Forest and /Forest/Trees here: it skips prims that are not defined, and a prim under an over ancestor is not defined. That keeps the prototypes from being treated as ordinary scene geometry.
Prototypes can live anywhere; placing them beneath the instancer is the usual practice.
protoIndices are zero-based, so [0, 1] gives the first tree Pine and the second Oak.

questions.stem: K1 and K2 are instanceable prims that payload kiosk.usda. The stage is opened with Usd.Stage.LoadNone, then stage.Load("/City/K1") is called. What do IsInstance() and stage.GetPrototypes() report before and after the Load?
options: Both are instances of one prototype throughout, because instanceable is read before payloads load.
Before: neither is an instance and there are no prototypes. After: K1 is an instance with one prototype; K2 is still not an instance.
Both become instances after the Load, because loading one payload loads the shared prototype.
LoadNone creates the prototypes, and Load fills them with the kiosk contents.
explanations: An instanceable prim whose payload is unloaded has nothing composed to share, so it is not an instance.
Load rules decide which payloads are composed. Only loaded instanceable prims get a prototype, so K2 joins once it is loaded too.
Loading is per prim path; K2's payload stays unloaded.
No prototype exists while every payload is unloaded.

questions.stem: stand.usda places three rows of row.usda: Row_01 and Row_02 are instanceable, Row_03 is not. Inside row.usda, the three seats are instanceable references to seat.usda. How many prototypes does the stage create?
explanations: Identical composition shares a prototype, so prototypes are not made per row or per seat.
Row_03's seats are instances of the same seat prototype; they do not add a third one.
One prototype serves the two instanced rows, and one seat prototype serves every seat instance: the seats inside the row prototype and the seats under the non-instanced Row_03.
Row content and seat content differ, so they cannot share a single prototype.

questions.stem: Inspection tools must recognize a fixed group of properties (inspector, inspection date, pass/fail) on existing Mesh, Xform and Camera prims, without changing those prims' types. Which kind of custom schema fits?
options: A new IsA (typed) schema that the prims are retyped to
A single-apply API schema, applied to the prims through apiSchemas metadata
A custom model kind
A new variant set added to every asset
explanations: A prim has exactly one type, so retyping would remove the Mesh, Xform or Camera behavior.
API schemas add named properties and behavior to prims of any type, and tools can test for them with HasAPI.
Kinds classify prims in the model hierarchy; they do not define properties.
Variant sets switch between alternatives; they are not a schema.

questions.stem: Which statements about generating custom schemas with usdGenSchema are correct? (Select TWO.)
