options: A codeless schema (skipCodeGeneration = true in the customData of schema.usda's GLOBAL prim) needs no compiled library; registering its generatedSchema.usda and plugInfo.json is enough.
Schema classes are described in a schema.usda file, from which usdGenSchema writes generatedSchema.usda and plugInfo.json (plus C++ and Python sources unless code generation is skipped).
An IsA schema is attached to a prim by listing its name in the prim's apiSchemas metadata.
Custom schemas only work after being merged into the core USD source tree.
usdGenSchema reads a JSON description and writes one USDA layer per asset that uses the schema.
explanations: Codeless schemas are easy to distribute because only the generated files and the plugin registration are needed.
This is the standard schema generation workflow.
IsA schemas set the prim's type name; apiSchemas lists applied API schemas.
Schemas are delivered as plugins discovered at runtime; the core does not need to change.
Its input is a USD layer (schema.usda), and it writes schema definitions and code, not asset layers.

questions.stem: Tools should treat a new model kind, "prop", as a kind of component, so that Kind.Registry.IsA("prop", "component") returns True. How is it registered?
options: Declare it in a plugin's plugInfo.json under Info > Kinds, with baseKind set to component.
Author kind = "prop" on a prim; USD infers the base kind from the prim's children.
Add "prop" to the apiSchemas list of each asset.
Define a class prim named _kind_prop in every asset layer.
explanations: The kind registry reads custom kinds and their base kinds from plugin metadata at startup.
Authoring an unknown kind does not register it, and base kinds are never inferred.
apiSchemas lists API schemas, not kinds.
Class prims are composition sources; they have nothing to do with the kind registry.

questions.stem: Your layers reference assets with identifiers such as studio:/props/chair?version=latest, and these must be turned into real file locations when layers are opened. Which OpenUSD extension point is designed for this?
options: A variant set that lists the possible file locations
A TfDebug symbol that rewrites paths
An Ar asset resolver plugin: an ArResolver subclass registered through plugInfo.json, as the primary resolver or for a URI scheme
A layer offset on every reference
explanations: Variants hold alternative scene description; path resolution happens in Ar before composition can even read the layer.
TfDebug only controls diagnostic output.
Ar decides how asset paths are resolved; a custom resolver can map studio identifiers to files, optionally using a resolver context.
Layer offsets retime layers; they do not resolve paths.

questions.stem: You built a schema plugin against the same USD version your application uses, but at runtime the new schema type is unknown. The plugin's files are installed outside the USD installation. What is the usual fix?
options: Add the folder containing the plugin's plugInfo.json to PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME before USD starts.
Copy schema.usda next to every layer that uses the schema.
Turn on TfDebug output for plugins, which registers missing plugins automatically.
Rename the compiled library to match the schema class name.
explanations: The plugin registry discovers plugins by searching that environment variable's paths for plugInfo.json files.
schema.usda is a build input; runtime discovery uses plugInfo.json and generatedSchema.usda.
Debug output (for example the PLUG_* symbols) helps you see what was found, but it does not register anything.
Library names are declared in plugInfo.json; renaming files does not make them discoverable.

questions.stem: You want Hydra to draw procedurally generated geometry, such as debug markers, without authoring any of it into USD layers. Which approach does Hydra 2.0 provide?
options: Mark the markers instanceable in the session layer
A scene index plugin (an HdSceneIndexPlugin registered with HdSceneIndexPluginRegistry) that adds or modifies Hydra prims in the scene index chain
Author the markers as over prims so they are never saved
Tag the markers with TfMallocTag so Hydra treats them as transient
explanations: The session layer is still a USD layer, and instancing does not generate geometry.
Scene index plugins filter or extend the scene that Hydra renders, independently of the USD stage.
Overs are still scene description in a layer, and prims that are only overs are not rendered.
TfMallocTag tracks memory allocations; it does not create geometry.

questions.stem: You are compiling OpenUSD from source so it can load inside a DCC that already ships its own TBB, Python and OpenSubdiv libraries. Why should the build use exactly those dependency versions instead of fetching its own?
options: USD refuses to compile unless every dependency is the newest release.
Only the imaging libraries depend on third-party code, so matching versions matters only for imaging.
Dependency versions affect only build time, never runtime behavior.
Two builds of one shared library, such as two TBBs, in one process can conflict or crash
explanations: USD documents supported dependency versions; it does not require the newest ones.
Core USD also needs third-party libraries, TBB for example.
Shared libraries are loaded at runtime, which is exactly where mismatches surface.
So USD must link against the libraries the host already loads. Studios commonly align such versions, for example with the VFX Reference Platform, and point the build at the host's libraries.

questions.stem: A headless asset-processing farm needs an OpenUSD build without imaging or usdview but with the Alembic file format plugin. Which approaches produce it? (Select TWO.)
options: python build_scripts/build_usd.py --no-imaging --alembic /opt/usd
Install usd-core from pip, then run it with --alembic to rebuild the Alembic plugin in place.
Build normally, then enable Alembic at runtime by adding its folder to PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME.
Set a PXR_BUILD_ALEMBIC_PLUGIN environment variable before running any USD tool.
Configure USD directly with CMake using -DPXR_BUILD_IMAGING=OFF -DPXR_BUILD_ALEMBIC_PLUGIN=ON, pointing CMake at already-built dependencies such as Alembic.
explanations: build_usd.py downloads and builds the required dependencies and USD into the install directory; --no-imaging also leaves out usdview, which needs imaging.
usd-core is a prebuilt wheel; it has no rebuild switch, and adding a plugin means compiling it.
The Alembic plugin must be compiled first; plugin paths only help the registry find plugins that exist.
PXR_BUILD_ALEMBIC_PLUGIN is a CMake option read at configure time, not a runtime environment variable.
Driving CMake yourself is how you build against dependencies you chose or built separately.

questions.stem: A small parameter file such as rocks.scatter (a seed and a count) should turn into Mesh prims whenever a layer references or payloads it, without any USD file being written to disk. Which extension point creates those prims?
options: An SdfFileFormat plugin whose Read() builds the layer in memory
A Hydra scene index plugin, because it adds prims to the USD stage.
A custom model kind with baseKind component.
An ArResolver whose Resolve() returns the generated prims.
explanations: A file format plugin registered in plugInfo.json for the .scatter extension fills an in-memory SdfLayer with generated prim specs, which then compose like any other layer. The resolver only locates the asset and hands over its bytes.
Scene indices add Hydra prims for rendering; USD queries and composition never see them.
Kinds categorize prims; they do not generate content.
Resolve() returns a resolved path, and OpenAsset() returns bytes; neither creates prim specs.

questions.stem: Your procedural file format plugin generates cubes whose count should come from the scene that uses them. Which statements about passing parameters to a file format plugin are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Layers generated by Read() must be saved to disk before they can be composed.
File format arguments are read from environment variables named after each argument.
Arguments can ride in the asset path, as in @cubes.proc:SDF_FORMAT_ARGS:count=10@
A dynamic file format can compute its arguments from metadata on the payload's prim
File formats can only be added by rebuilding USD, because Sdf does not load them from plugins.
explanations: Generated layers live in memory and compose directly.
Arguments travel with the layer identifier (or are computed by a dynamic file format), not through environment variables.
Sdf.Layer.SplitIdentifier separates the path from the arguments. Layers opened with different arguments are distinct layers, so each argument set gets its own generated content.

An SdfFileFormat that also implements PcpDynamicFileFormatInterface reads metadata on the prim that holds the payload, so editing that metadata regenerates the content. This is how parameters authored in the scene drive procedural payload content.
File formats are ordinary plugins found through plugInfo.json.

questions.stem: A schema plugin compiled against OpenUSD 25.05 fails to load in an application that bundles OpenUSD 25.11, with errors about unresolved symbols. What is the cause and the fix?
options: The plugin's folder is missing from PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME; adding it resolves the symbols.
plugInfo.json needs a "UsdVersion": "25.11" entry so the registry can translate the symbols.
USD makes no ABI promise and versions its symbol namespace, so rebuild against 25.11
The library file name must end with the USD version number.
explanations: If the folder were missing, the plugin would not be found at all; unresolved symbols mean it was found but cannot link.
There is no such key; the registry cannot adapt a binary built for another release.

C++ symbols live in a versioned internal namespace (pxrInternal_v0_25_11__pxrReserved__ in a default 25.11 build), so the plugin must be rebuilt against the application's exact USD build and options. pxr/pxr.h also defines PXR_VERSION, so code can check which release it is compiled against.
Library names are whatever plugInfo.json declares; renaming files does not fix linking.

questions.stem: An exporter tags hero assets with kind = "hero", but nobody registered that kind. What do Usd.ModelAPI(chair).GetKind() and chair.IsModel() report for /Set/Chair?
options: "hero" and True, because any authored kind makes a prim a model.
"hero" and False: the kind is kept, but the registry does not know it
"" and False, because unregistered kinds are dropped when the layer is read.
"component" and True, because USD maps unknown kinds to component.
explanations: Model status depends on the kind registry knowing that the kind derives from model.
Unregistered kinds are just tokens to the registry, so IsA checks against model fail and model-hierarchy tools skip the chair. Registering "hero" in plugInfo.json with baseKind component fixes that.
The authored token is kept; only its meaning is unknown.
USD never guesses a base kind.

questions.stem: An importer maps a DCC's per-object mass onto the built-in UsdPhysics MassAPI instead of an ad hoc attribute, producing the prim below. Which statements are true? (Select TWO.)
options: physics:mass is ignored, because properties of API schemas must be declared custom.
prim.GetAppliedSchemas() includes "PhysicsMassAPI", so tools can find every prim that carries mass data.
Applying the API schema changes the prim's type from Cube to PhysicsMassAPI.
Without the apiSchemas entry, the authored physics:mass could no longer be read.
prim.GetAttribute("physics:density") is valid and returns the schema's fallback, 0.0, even though no layer authors it.
explanations: Schema properties are normally authored without custom; the value 3 composes.
Applied schemas are queryable (for example with HasAPI), which ad hoc attributes are not.
API schemas are added alongside the prim's single type; the prim stays a Cube.
Authored attributes can always be read; the schema adds meaning and fallbacks, not the data itself.
Applied schemas contribute their built-in properties and fallback values to the prim definition.

scenarios.note: same attribute without the applied schema

questions.stem: A filtering scene index inserts a procedural debug mesh at /Debug/Marker into the Hydra scene it passes downstream. What must it do so that downstream scene indices and the render delegate draw the mesh?
options: Author a UsdGeomMesh at /Debug/Marker in the stage's session layer from inside the scene index.
Mark /Debug/Marker instanceable so that Hydra creates it on demand.
Call stage.Reload() so the scene index chain is rebuilt with the marker.
Send PrimsAdded for it and serve it from GetChildPrimPaths and GetPrim with mesh data sources
explanations: Scene indices work on Hydra data, not on USD layers; writing to the stage defeats the purpose.
Instancing metadata belongs to USD prims and does not create Hydra prims.
Reload rereads layers from disk; it has nothing to do with procedural Hydra prims.

Downstream observers learn about prims through PrimsAdded notices (prim type mesh) and read their data through GetPrim, which returns an HdSceneIndexPrim whose container data source holds the topology and points, for example through HdMeshSchema and HdPrimvarsSchema.

questions.stem: In schema.usda you are describing SocketAPI, which one prim may carry several times under different instance names, giving properties such as socket:left:offset and socket:right:offset. How is the class declared?
options: It inherits </APISchemaBase> and sets customData apiSchemaType = "multipleApply" with propertyNamespacePrefix = "socket".
It inherits </Typed> and is marked instanceable = true.
Write one single-apply class per instance name (SocketLeftAPI, SocketRightAPI, ...).
It sets apiSchemaType = "nonApplied" and lists the instance names in a variant set.
explanations: usdGenSchema then generates a schema applied as SocketAPI:<instance>, with properties named socket:<instance>:<name>.
Typed schemas define prim types, and instanceable is unrelated composition metadata.
That fixes the list of instances at schema build time, which a multiple-apply schema avoids.
Non-applied schemas are never recorded on prims, and variant sets are not part of schema definitions.

questions.stem: Which statements correctly compare the .usda and .usdc encodings? (Select TWO.)
options: usda is human-readable text, convenient for small interface layers, diffs and code review.
Some scene description, such as time samples, can only be stored in usda.
usdc layers cannot be referenced from usda layers.
Converting a layer from usda to usdc changes how it composes.
usdc (crate) is binary; it opens faster and can memory-map large arrays, which suits heavy geometry.
explanations: Text layers are easy to inspect and compare, so they suit lightweight aggregation layers.
Both encodings store the same scene description, time samples included.
Layers of any encoding can reference, sublayer or payload each other.
The data model is identical, so composition results do not depend on the encoding.
Crate is designed for fast loading and low memory use with data-heavy layers.

questions.stem: A script calls Usd.Stage.CreateNew("asset.usd"), defines some prims and saves. With default settings, which encoding does the saved .usd file use?
options: A zip package (usdz)
Binary crate (usdc)
Whichever encoding the most recently opened layer used
Text (usda)
explanations: A .usd file is never written as a zip package. Sdf treats usdz as read-only, so even Stage.CreateNew("asset.usdz") fails; packages are assembled from finished layers with usdzip or UsdUtils.CreateNewUsdzPackage.

A .usd file can hold either encoding, and new .usd files are written as crate by default. The file's first bytes tell you which one it uses (PXR-USDC for crate, #usda for text); usdcat prints text to stdout whatever the source encoding.
The default does not depend on other layers in the session.
Text is the default only when you name the file .usda.

questions.stem: Which command writes a text copy of a binary layer for inspection, without flattening its composition?
options: usdzip model.usdc model.usda
usdresolve model.usdc model.usda
usdchecker model.usdc --out model.usda
usdcat model.usdc -o model.usda
explanations: usdzip creates .usdz packages.
usdresolve prints how an asset path resolves.
usdchecker validates assets; it does not convert them.
usdcat writes the layer in the format implied by the output extension; composition is preserved unless --flatten is given.

questions.stem: You are writing an automated check for assets exported from a DCC. Which tools or APIs are suitable building blocks? (Select TWO.)
options: Sdf.ChangeBlock, which rolls back edits that would make an asset invalid
usdchecker, which validates a stage or .usdz package against a set of rules and reports failures
UsdUtils.ComputeAllDependencies, which reports the layers and assets an asset uses, including paths that do not resolve
usdcat --flatten, which prints validation errors for the composed stage
explanations: Change blocks only batch change notifications; they do not validate or roll back.
usdchecker is the stock validation tool and is easy to run in a pipeline or CI job.
Listing unresolved paths catches broken references and missing textures before publishing.
usdcat converts or flattens layers; it is not a validator.

questions.stem: Your validator inspects the exported panel below. Which problems should it report? (Select TWO.)
options: The authored extent does not enclose the points; it should be [(0, 0, 0), (2, 2, 0)].
faceVertexIndices refers to point 5, but only points 0 to 3 exist.
faceVertexCounts must contain one entry per point.
A Mesh must author normals to be valid.
kind = "component" is not allowed on an Xform.
explanations: extent must bound the points; a stale extent breaks culling and framing.
Every face-vertex index must address an existing entry of points.
faceVertexCounts has one entry per face; here one quad, so [4] is right.
normals are optional; renderers can compute them.
Kind is model metadata and is commonly authored on an asset's root Xform.

questions.stem: You are writing a conceptual data-mapping document between MaterialX and UsdShade. Which mapping is correct?
options: A MaterialX nodegraph maps to a UsdGeomSubset.
A MaterialX surfacematerial maps to a UsdLux light.
A MaterialX nodegraph maps to a UsdShadeNodeGraph prim, and its nodes map to UsdShadeShader prims.
Each MaterialX node maps to its own variant set.
explanations: GeomSubsets partition geometry elements; they do not represent shading graphs.
A surfacematerial corresponds to a UsdShadeMaterial.
This mirrors how the usdMtlx plugin represents MaterialX documents in USD.
Variant sets hold alternatives, not shading nodes.

questions.stem: A converter brings glTF 2.0 files into USD. Which stage metadata should it author so the result keeps glTF's coordinate conventions?
options: No metadata is needed; USD reads glTF units at render time
upAxis = "Y" and metersPerUnit = 1.0
upAxis = "Y" and metersPerUnit = 0.01
upAxis = "Z" and metersPerUnit = 0.01
explanations: Unit and axis intent are only known if the converter authors them (otherwise USD fallbacks apply).
glTF content is Y-up and measured in meters; authoring both makes that intent explicit to USD consumers.
The axis matches, but 0.01 declares centimeters while glTF uses meters.
That describes Z-up centimeters, not glTF.

questions.stem: When converting a USD asset to glTF 2.0, which steps help preserve fidelity? (Select TWO.)
options: Keep every custom primvar as-is; glTF stores arbitrary USD primvars with all their interpolations.
Write the glTF as a USD sublayer so composition is preserved.
Map UsdPreviewSurface inputs such as diffuseColor, metallic and roughness onto glTF's metallic-roughness material, and report shading that cannot be mapped.
Skip unit and axis conversion because glTF reads metersPerUnit and upAxis from the file.
Export the composed result (with the intended variant selections), since glTF has no equivalent of references, payloads or variant sets.
explanations: glTF has a fixed set of vertex attributes; arbitrary primvars and interpolations need mapping or are lost.
A glTF file is not a USD layer, and sublayering does not apply to the output format.
Material mapping is where conversions most often lose fidelity, so make the mapping explicit.
glTF has fixed conventions (Y-up, meters), so the converter must convert explicitly.
Composition has to be resolved before export; decide and document which variants are baked.

questions.stem: Artists import a USD asset into a DCC, edit it, and export it back. Which practices help this round trip preserve data? (Select TWO.)
options: Rename prims on each export to include the export date.
Keep stable prim names and paths so re-exported data lands on the prims it came from.
Flatten the stage on every export and replace the original asset files with the result.
Write the DCC's changes as overrides into a dedicated layer instead of overwriting the source layers.
Drop attributes the DCC does not understand to keep exports clean.
explanations: Changing paths breaks every opinion that targets the old paths.
Stable paths let downstream overrides and references keep working after each export.
That destroys the layer and arc structure other people depend on.
Sparse overrides in a separate layer are non-destructive and keep other departments' work intact.
Silently discarding unknown data is the classic round-trip loss.

questions.stem: An importer gets the attribute below with prop = prim.GetProperty("studio:inspection:weight"). What do prop.GetNamespace() and prop.GetBaseName() return?
options: "studio" and "inspection:weight"
"studio:inspection:" and "weight"
"" and "studio:inspection:weight", because only schema attributes have namespaces
"studio:inspection" and "weight"
explanations: The split happens at the last delimiter, not the first.
The returned namespace has no trailing delimiter.
Namespaces are part of any property name, custom or not.
The namespace is everything before the last ':' delimiter, and the base name is the last part.

questions.stem: Your exporter writes content from a Z-up application. Which call records that on the new stage?
options: stage.SetUpAxis("Z")
UsdGeom.Xform.Define(stage, "/Z")
UsdGeom.SetStageUpAxis(stage, UsdGeom.Tokens.z)
Rotate every exported prim by 90 degrees around X and leave upAxis unauthored
explanations: UsdStage has no SetUpAxis method; axis handling lives in UsdGeom.
That just defines a prim named Z.
UsdGeom provides helpers for the upAxis stage metadata (and SetStageMetersPerUnit for units).
Baking a rotation changes the data and still leaves consumers guessing the intended axis.

questions.stem: An exporter writes a 48-frame animation of a prop's translation. Which steps are appropriate? (Select TWO.)
options: Write one time sample per frame, for example translate_op.Set(value, Usd.TimeCode(frame)).
Create one prim per frame and toggle their visibility.
Author startTimeCode and endTimeCode, and set timeCodesPerSecond to the DCC's frame rate.
Store all 48 positions in the attribute's default value and let USD pick one per frame.
Set timeCodesPerSecond to 48 because the animation has 48 frames.
explanations: Animated values are stored as time samples keyed by time code.
That multiplies prims instead of animating one attribute.
These layer metadata tell players the playback range and how time codes map to seconds.
A default value is a single, time-independent value; USD does not index into it by frame.
timeCodesPerSecond is a rate, not a frame count.

questions.stem: An importer loops over `for prim in stage.Traverse()` on the layer below. Which paths does it visit, in order?
options: /World, /World/Crate, /World/Archive
/World, /World/Crate
/World, /World/Crate, /World/Archive, /World/Archive/OldCrate, /_class_Prop, /Notes
/World, /World/Crate, /_class_Prop
explanations: Inactive prims are skipped by the default predicate.
The default predicate visits only active, loaded, defined, non-abstract prims. /World/Archive is inactive (and its children are not composed), the class is abstract, and /Notes is only an over.
This would need a traversal with an all-prims predicate, and even then the children of an inactive prim are not composed.
Class prims are abstract and skipped by default.

questions.stem: Your importer brings the layer below into a DCC whose scene unit is the meter. Based on UsdGeom.GetStageMetersPerUnit(stage), what uniform scale should it apply to positions to keep their real-world size?
options: It depends on upAxis, because Z-up layers are always stored in meters
1, because USD positions are always stored in meters
explanations: upAxis and metersPerUnit are independent pieces of metadata.
USD stores positions in the layer's declared units, here centimeters.
metersPerUnit = 0.01 means one unit is a centimeter, so multiplying by 0.01 converts to meters.
That would convert meters to centimeters, the opposite direction.

questions.stem: An exporter must carry a per-face integer "damageZone" value from the DCC so downstream tools can read it through the primvar API. Which authoring choice is correct for a Mesh?
options: A string attribute containing the values separated by commas
An int[] primvar (primvars:damageZone) with interpolation "uniform", holding one value per face
An int[] primvar with interpolation "vertex", holding one value per face
A custom metadata key on the mesh prim listing the values
explanations: Strings hide the structure from primvar-aware tools and renderers.
For meshes, uniform interpolation means one element per face.
vertex interpolation expects one element per point, not per face.
Metadata is not meant for per-element data, and new metadata keys must be registered.

questions.stem: shot.usda sublayers an artist's round-trip export (layout_edits.usda) above the published model.usda. In the DCC the artist only raised the seat, but the exporter wrote back every Seat attribute it had imported. Modeling has since republished model.usda with size = 2. What does /Chair/Seat.size compose to, and what does that reveal?

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    defaultPrim = "Chair"
    subLayers = [
        @./layout_edits.usda@,
        @./model.usda@
    ]
)

options: 2, because the most recently saved layer always wins.
2, because a def in a weaker layer overrides opinions authored in a stronger layer.
No value, because two sublayers that both def the same prim cause a composition error.
1, because the export copied the old size into the stronger layer; the exporter should write only the properties the artist changed.
explanations: Strength comes from the order of the subLayers list, not from file timestamps.
Specifiers do not change strength; the stronger layer's opinion wins whether it was written with def or over.
Several layers may define the same prim; their opinions are merged by strength without any error.

layout_edits.usda is listed first, so its stale size = 1 beats the republished value. A sparse export (an over that authors only the new translate) lets later upstream changes such as size = 2 show through.

scenarios.note: sparse export that authors only the moved translate

questions.stem: A DCC plugin imports a shot whose props are referenced from published assets with variant selections, and whose camera is keyframed. After the artist edits the shot, the plugin exports it again. Which export behaviors keep the shot's USD structure and data intact? (Select TWO.)
options: Write each prop's composed geometry into the shot layer so the shot no longer depends on the published assets.
Author the references and variant selections again on the same prim paths, instead of the geometry they produced.
Set instanceable = false on every prop, because DCC objects are always unique copies.
Convert only the exported shot layer to the DCC's up axis and leave the referenced assets as they are.
Write the camera's animation as time samples (one per keyed or evaluated frame) rather than a single default value.
explanations: Baking the composed result throws away the references, so later fixes to the published assets never reach the shot.
Re-authoring the arcs keeps the shot lightweight and linked to the published assets, exactly as it was imported.
That silently changes how the shot is instanced; the round trip should carry the instanceable metadata through unchanged.
Mixing axis conventions between a layer and the assets it references misplaces content; axis handling must be consistent.
Time samples preserve the animation; a lone default value would keep just one pose.

questions.stem: A first version of a DCC importer reads every attribute with attr.Get() and no time argument. Which value does it read for /Prop.xformOp:translate below, and what happens to the animation when the scene is exported again?
options: (0, 0, 0), the default value, so the re-export loses the animation
(14, 0, 0), the last time sample; only the end pose survives.
(8, 0, 0), the value halfway through the frame range.
(2, 0, 0), the first time sample, because samples always beat defaults.
explanations: Get() without a time asks for Usd.TimeCode.Default(), which returns the authored default and ignores time samples. The time samples are never read, so the importer must also call attr.GetTimeSamples() and evaluate Get(t) at each of those times to keep the animation.
The last sample is what Get(24) returns, not Get() with no time.
That is Get(12) with linear interpolation; a call without a time does not interpolate.
Samples win only when a numeric time is requested; the default time code reads the default value.

questions.stem: door.usda used to place the door with xformOp:translate = (2, 0, 0) followed by xformOp:rotateZ, and anim.usda opens it with rotateZ = 90. After a DCC round trip, door.usda was re-exported with both ops collapsed into one xformOp:transform matrix, as shown. Where is /Door/Handle in world space on the shot.usda stage now?

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    defaultPrim = "Door"
    subLayers = [
        @./anim.usda@,
        @./door.usda@
    ]
)

options: (2, 1, 0), because anim.usda's rotateZ is still the strongest opinion.
(1, 0, 0), because the matrix op replaces the transforms that children inherit.
(3, 0, 0): xformOpOrder now lists only xformOp:transform, so the animator's rotateZ is ignored; a round trip should keep the original op stack.
(2, 0, 0), because the matrix moves the door and the handle together to the door's origin.
explanations: That was the result before the round trip. The opinion still composes, but an op that is not listed in xformOpOrder has no effect.
A child's world transform is its local transform combined with its parent's; the door's matrix still moves the handle.
Only ops named in xformOpOrder contribute, so the handle is just offset by the matrix's translation of 2. Keeping op names and order stable lets downstream layers keep overriding individual ops.
(2, 0, 0) is the door's own origin; the handle adds its local offset of (1, 0, 0).

questions.stem: A glTF exporter walks the composed stage of car.usda with stage.Traverse() and writes every Mesh prim it visits. Which meshes end up in the glTF file?
options: Body_high, Body_low and Wheels, because exporters see the contents of every variant.
Body_low and Wheels: the stage composes only the selected "low" variant, so the export bakes that choice.
Wheels only, because prims inside variants are skipped until the variant set is flattened.
Body_high and Wheels, because exporters use the first variant authored.
explanations: Only the selected variant's opinions are composed; the other variant's prims do not exist on the stage.
glTF has no variant sets, so the exporter writes whatever the current selection produces. To export another LOD, change the selection (for example in the session layer) before exporting.
Prims from the selected variant are ordinary composed prims and are visited by Traverse.
The authored selection ("low") decides; variant order in the file does not.

scenarios.note: selection switched to high before export

questions.stem: You are documenting what a USD-to-glTF 2.0 converter can carry across. Which statements are correct? (Select THREE.)
options: glTF vertex attributes are stored per vertex, so faceVarying data such as UVs with seams requires splitting vertices.
glTF stores Catmull-Clark subdivision surfaces natively, so subdivisionScheme can be copied unchanged.
Core glTF animation channels can target any property, so every time-sampled USD attribute becomes a channel.
Several glTF nodes can use the same mesh, so instances of one USD prototype can be written once and placed many times.
glTF understands USD's purpose attribute, so guide and proxy prims are filtered out automatically.
The core glTF material is metallic-roughness PBR, so a UsdPreviewSurface that uses the specular workflow needs conversion or an extension.
explanations: A point with different UVs on neighboring faces must become several glTF vertices.
Core glTF has no subdivision surfaces; the converter must tessellate (refine) the mesh or accept that it renders as the cage.
Core channels target node translation, rotation, scale and morph-target weights; other animated data needs baking or extensions.
Mesh reuse across nodes preserves much of the memory benefit of USD instancing.
glTF has no purpose concept; the converter must decide which purposes to export.
useSpecularWorkflow = 1 has no direct core-glTF equivalent; the mapping must be documented and converted.

questions.stem: Your exporter writes glTF 2.0, which is Y-up and measured in meters. It converts Z-up data with the right-handed mapping (x, y, z) -> (x, z, -y), a -90 degree rotation about X. Where should /Rig/Sensor end up in glTF world space?
explanations: The units are converted, but the axis change was skipped.
The axes are swapped, but metersPerUnit = 0.01 means centimeters, so every coordinate must also be multiplied by 0.01.
This drops the parent's translation; the world position includes /Rig's (100, 0, 0).
This rotates the wrong way; with the stated mapping the new Y is the old Z and the new Z is minus the old Y.
The world position is (100, 200, 50) in centimeters, (1, 2, 0.5) in meters, and (1, 0.5, -2) after mapping Z-up to Y-up.

questions.stem: A DCC stores each object as a transform node with a separate shape node (the geometry) beneath it. Which statement belongs in your DCC-to-USD mapping document?
options: USD meshes cannot carry transforms, so every shape must sit under its own Xform prim.
The shape node maps to a relationship on the Xform that targets the geometry data.
Transform nodes map to Scope prims, because Scope is USD's grouping prim.
A transform with one shape can become a single Mesh prim carrying the xformOps
explanations: Mesh inherits from Xformable, so it can hold xformOps itself.
Geometry is a prim (a Mesh, for example), not a relationship target on a transform.
Scope is not xformable; a grouping node that carries a transform maps to an Xform.

Gprims such as Mesh are xformable, so one prim can hold both. An Xform parent is still useful when one transform holds several shapes; both layouts are valid USD, and the mapping document should state which one the converter uses and when.

questions.stem: In MaterialX, a parameter exposed on a material drives an input of a node inside it. In the UsdShade network below, which construct plays that role, and how does the shader receive the value?
options: The Material's own input inputs:baseTint, which diffuseColor connects to
A primvar on the bound mesh, which the shader reads through the material binding.
customData on the Material that renderers copy into the shader at render time.
A variant set on the Material with one variant per tint.
explanations: Inputs on a Material form its public interface; the shader's connected diffuseColor input takes its value from it, so users edit the value on the Material without touching the shader.
Primvars are read with primvar reader shaders; the network here uses a connection to a Material input.
customData is not part of shading; renderers do not read shader values from it.
Variants could switch whole looks, but the exposed parameter itself is a Material input.

questions.stem: Which entries in a DCC-to-USD mapping document are accurate? (Select TWO.)
options: DCC display layers (groups used to show or hide objects) map to sublayers.
A DCC frame range maps to the layer offset of each reference.
DCC object sets (named groups of objects) map to CollectionAPI instances, which list included and excluded paths.
DCC group nodes that carry a transform map to Scope prims.
Many copies of one DCC geometry, each with its own transform, map to scenegraph instancing (instanceable references) or a PointInstancer.
explanations: Sublayers are composition layers holding opinions; a display grouping maps to visibility, purpose or a collection.
Playback range maps to the layer's startTimeCode and endTimeCode; layer offsets shift or scale time.
Collections are the USD way to name a set of prims and properties.
Scope has no transform; such groups map to Xform prims.
Both are USD's instancing mechanisms; which one fits depends on how much per-copy control is needed.

questions.stem: Your DCC exports the prim below using an in-house StudioInspectionAPI schema. A partner studio without your schema plugin imports the file. Which statements are true on the partner's side? (Select TWO.)
options: prim.GetAttribute("studio:inspector").Get() still returns "Ana".
Usd.Stage.Open fails, because the layer names an unregistered schema.
prim.HasAPI("StudioInspectionAPI") returns True, because the name is listed in apiSchemas.
prim.GetAppliedSchemas() returns only ["MaterialBindingAPI"]; the unknown name stays in the authored apiSchemas metadata but adds no schema definition.
USD removes the unknown name from apiSchemas when the stage opens, so re-saving the layer loses it.
explanations: Authored attributes do not depend on any schema; the value composes and can be read.
Unknown API schema names do not stop a stage from opening.
HasAPI only reports schemas that are applied and known to the schema registry.
Applied schemas are filtered through the registry, so the unknown entry contributes no fallbacks or built-in properties.
Opening a stage never edits its layers; the metadata is written back as authored.

questions.stem: An exporter turns a DCC object's named selection groups into the CollectionAPI entries below. Which statement is correct?
options: A prim can apply CollectionAPI only once, so the "lights" entry replaces "wheels".
Instance names such as "wheels" must be registered in a plugInfo.json before they can be used.
CollectionAPI is multiple-apply: each instance name gets its own collection:<name>: properties
API schemas cannot add relationships, so the members must be stored as child Scope prims.
explanations: CollectionAPI is designed to be applied many times on one prim.
Instance names are picked when the schema is applied (any valid name the schema does not reserve); only the schema itself is registered.
Multiple-apply schemas let one prim carry any number of named groups without clashing property names; GetAppliedSchemas() lists both CollectionAPI:wheels and CollectionAPI:lights.
includes and excludes are relationships defined by CollectionAPI itself.

questions.stem: An exporter wrote a DCC locator as a prim of type StudioLocator, a type no schema plugin defines, and gave it xformOps as shown. Where do consumers place /World/Marker/Tip in world space?
options: At (10, 0, 0): StudioLocator is not Xformable, so its ops are ignored
At (10, 5, 0): authored xformOps always apply, whatever the prim type.
Nowhere: the stage fails to open because the prim type is unknown.
Nowhere: Traverse skips prims of unknown type, so Tip is never visited.
explanations: Transform semantics come from the Xformable schema, not from attributes that happen to be named xformOp. The prim keeps its type name; exporting it as an Xform, with the extra data in namespaced attributes or an API schema, avoids this.
Only Xformable prims contribute a local transform; an unknown type is not Xformable.
Unknown type names do not prevent composition; the prim simply has no schema behind it.
Traverse visits defined, active, loaded prims whatever their type; Marker and Tip are both visited.

questions.stem: A publish check runs on lamp.usda straight out of a DCC. It must catch anything that would break a consumer that references the file without a prim path or that tessellates the mesh. Which findings are genuine? (Select TWO.)
options: points must have as many entries as faceVertexIndices.
defaultPrim "Lamp" does not match the root prim "lamp"
faceVertexCounts sums to 6, but there are 5 indices
A component's root prim must be a Mesh rather than an Xform.
upAxis must be "Y" for the asset to be valid.
explanations: Indices may reuse points; points needs one entry per vertex, not per face-vertex.
Prim names are case-sensitive, so stage.GetDefaultPrim() is invalid and a reference to the file without a prim path finds no target. The metadata must name an existing root prim exactly.
The sum of faceVertexCounts must equal the length of faceVertexIndices; UsdGeom.Mesh.ValidateTopology reports this mismatch.
Component roots are commonly Xforms that group the asset's geometry.
Z-up is valid; the validator should check that upAxis is authored, not that it is Y.

scenarios.note: defaultPrim spelled like the root prim

questions.stem: Your validator must fail car.usda when, as here, wheel.usda was never delivered. Which check does that?
options: Wrap Usd.Stage.Open in try/except and fail on an exception.
Fail when stage.GetPrimAtPath("/Car/Wheel").IsValid() is False.
Fail when /Car/Wheel's HasAuthoredReferences() is False.
Fail when stage.GetCompositionErrors() is non-empty.
explanations: Open succeeds; an unresolved reference raises nothing and is only reported as a warning.
car.usda still defines /Car/Wheel, so the prim stays valid and this check passes the broken asset.
The reference is authored, so this check passes the broken asset.
The missing asset is recorded as a composition error, which is data to check, not an exception. UsdUtils.ComputeAllDependencies also lists wheel.usda among the unresolved paths.

questions.stem: A DCC exporter marks both crates instanceable = true, expecting them to share one prototype, but writes each crate's geometry inline. What does a validator find on the composed stage?
options: Both crates are instances of one shared prototype.
Neither crate is an instance, and the stage has no prototypes
Each crate becomes an instance with its own prototype.
The stage fails to compose, because instanceable prims cannot have children of their own.
explanations: Instancing shares content that arrives through composition arcs; inline children are not shared.

Instancing only applies to prims that get their content through composition arcs. An instanceable prim without arcs is composed like any other prim, so the flag has no effect here; the exporter should reference a shared asset or prototype prim instead.
No prototypes are created at all, since there is nothing composed to share.
Nothing fails; the metadata is simply inert on prims without arcs.

scenarios.note: crates reference a shared class prim

questions.stem: Your importer should create one DCC mesh per unique piece of instanced geometry and place a lightweight DCC instance for each USD instance. Which approach does that for the yard below?
options: Traverse with Usd.TraverseInstanceProxies() and convert every Box it finds into its own mesh.
Copy the _Crate class into the DCC, because class prims are the prototypes the stage instances.
Convert only the prims returned by stage.GetPrototypes(), because prototypes also carry each instance's transform.
Convert each distinct GetPrototype() of the instance prims once, then place one DCC instance per USD instance
explanations: That visits each instance's proxies and duplicates the geometry once per crate.
The class is only the source of the reference arc; the stage builds its own prototypes, and classes are not rendered.
Per-instance transforms live on the instance prims, so they must be read there.
Instances that share composition share a prototype, so each prototype's subtree is converted once and reused; each DCC instance takes its transform from its own instance prim.

questions.stem: Your team archives finished assets for years and wants them reviewable and loadable later. Which statements about .usda and .usdc are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Re-saving a .usda drops # comments; keep archive notes in doc or customLayerData
A .usda file is always smaller than the same data written as .usdc.
Crate cannot hold custom layer metadata such as customLayerData.
Text must be parsed in full on open; crate can read large values on demand
Crate rewrites relative asset paths as absolute, so .usdc archives break if moved
explanations: The text parser discards # comments, so a re-save loses them; layer metadata such as doc or customLayerData survives in both encodings.
Text is usually larger, especially for big numeric arrays.
Both encodings store the same scene description, metadata included.
Crate's layout allows lazy, memory-mapped access, which is why it opens heavy layers faster.
Both encodings store asset paths exactly as authored; @./tex/a.png@ reads back unchanged from a .usdc. Only flattening anchors relative paths.

questions.stem: A Python converter holds an Sdf.Layer and must deliver it as asset.usd that reviewers can read as text. Which call does that?
options: layer.Export("asset.usd", args={"format": "usda"})
layer.Export("asset.usd"), because a .usd file keeps the source layer's encoding.
layer.Export("asset.usd", args={"encoding": "text"})
It cannot be done, because a .usd file is always crate.
explanations: The usd file format accepts a format argument of usda or usdc for .usd files.
New .usd files are written as crate by default, even when the source layer was text.
encoding is not an argument the usd format reads; it is ignored and the file is still written as crate.
A .usd file may hold either encoding; readers detect it from the file's first bytes.

questions.stem: A DCC object is called "Left Door-01", which is not a valid prim name. The exporter wrote the prim below. Which statement describes a sound naming scheme for the round trip?
options: Prim names may contain spaces and hyphens when they are quoted in USDA, so the original name could have been kept.
The exporter should skip such objects, because names that need conversion cannot be represented in USD.
Tf.MakeValidIdentifier("Left Door-01") gives "Left_Door_01" for the prim name, and the original label goes into the prim's displayName metadata so an importer can restore it.
Store the original name as the prim's kind so model-hierarchy tools can show it.
explanations: Quotes do not relax the rule: prim names must be valid identifiers.
Converting the name and storing the label elsewhere keeps the object.
The conversion cannot be reversed on its own, and two DCC names can collide after it, so the exporter must also keep the label and make names unique among siblings.
kind classifies prims in the model hierarchy; it is not a label.

questions.stem: An exporter builds its layer with the Sdf API: Sdf.CreatePrimInLayer(layer, "/Robot/Arm") followed by attribute specs, and saves the result shown. Opening it, stage.Traverse() visits nothing. Why?
options: Layers authored through Sdf stay invisible to Usd until the stage is reloaded.
CreatePrimInLayer makes untyped overs, and Traverse() skips undefined prims
Attribute specs must be created before their prim specs.
The layer has no defaultPrim, and Traverse starts at the default prim.
explanations: Usd sees Sdf edits immediately; the prims are there, just not defined.

Sdf.CreatePrimInLayer creates over specs without a type, for the prim and any missing ancestors. Overs only hold opinions: TraverseAll() would list /Robot and /Robot/Arm, but Traverse() skips them. Set each spec's specifier to Sdf.SpecifierDef and give it a typeName such as Xform.
The order of spec creation does not matter.
Traverse starts at the pseudo-root and never consults defaultPrim, which is read when another layer references or payloads this one without a prim path.

questions.stem: You add a float[] primvar named primvars:wear with 8 values to the Ribbon mesh below. Which interpolation makes 8 the correct number of elements?

usda.ribbon.usda:
#usda 1.0

def Mesh "Ribbon"
{
    float3[] extent = [(0, 0, 0), (2, 1, 0)]
    int[] faceVertexCounts = [4, 4]
    int[] faceVertexIndices = [0, 1, 4, 3, 1, 2, 5, 4]
    point3f[] points = [(0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (2, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (1, 1, 0), (2, 1, 0)]
}

options: faceVarying
uniform
constant
vertex
explanations: faceVarying needs one value per face-vertex: two quads give 8 face-vertices, the length of faceVertexIndices.
uniform needs one value per face, which is 2 here.
constant needs a single value for the whole mesh.
vertex needs one value per point, which is 6 here.

questions.stem: Which Python call adds a texture-coordinate primvar named st, with one value per face-vertex, to `mesh` (a UsdGeom.Mesh)?
options: UsdGeom.PrimvarsAPI(mesh).CreatePrimvar("st", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.String, UsdGeom.Tokens.constant)
UsdGeom.PrimvarsAPI(mesh).CreatePrimvar("st", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.TexCoord2fArray, UsdGeom.Tokens.faceVarying)
mesh.GetPrim().CreateAttribute("st", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.TexCoord2fArray)
mesh.CreateDisplayColorAttr("st")
explanations: A single string is the wrong type and the wrong interpolation for texture coordinates.
PrimvarsAPI creates the primvars:st attribute with the right role type and interpolation metadata.
This creates a plain attribute called st outside the primvars: namespace, so it is not a primvar and has no interpolation.
That creates the displayColor attribute; the argument is a default value, not a name.

questions.stem: Which value-type choices are appropriate? (Select TWO.)
options: matrix4d for an xformOp:transform operation
token for a value chosen from a small fixed set of names, such as a mode switch
one double to hold a separate radius for each of 10,000 points
string[] to store vertex positions
int to store a linear RGB color
explanations: A transform op stores a full 4x4 matrix, and its type is matrix4d.
Tokens are interned strings meant for identifiers and enumerated choices.
Per-element data needs an array type, such as float[] for widths.
Positions are point3f[] so tools know their role.
Colors use color3f (or color3d/color3h).

questions.stem: Which declaration matches how UsdGeomPointBased stores per-point velocities?
options: color3f[] velocities
vector3f[] velocities
point3f[] velocities
normal3f[] velocities
explanations: The color role is for colors.
Velocities are directions, so they use the vector role, which is transformed without translation.
The point role is for positions; translations would wrongly apply to them.
The normal role is for surface normals, which transform differently from vectors.

questions.stem: What does prim.GetCustomDataByKey("review:status") return for the Valve prim below?
options: "approved"
None, because nested dictionaries cannot be addressed by key
An error, because ':' is not allowed in keys
The whole review dictionary
explanations: Key paths use ':' to reach into nested dictionaries inside customData.
GetCustomDataByKey accepts ':'-separated key paths into nested dictionaries.
':' is the key-path separator here.
That is what GetCustomDataByKey("review") returns.

questions.stem: You need to record studio notes (reviewer, ticket number) on prims without writing or deploying any plugin. Which mechanism is designed for this?
options: The apiSchemas list
The customData dictionary metadata
prim.SetMetadata("reviewer", "kim") with a new top-level metadata key
The kind metadata
explanations: apiSchemas lists applied API schemas, not notes.
customData holds arbitrary user dictionaries on prims and properties and needs no registration.
SetMetadata only accepts registered fields; a new field must first be registered through a plugin (SdfMetadata in plugInfo.json).
kind classifies prims in the model hierarchy.

questions.stem: Which statements about the Ball prim's properties are true? (Select TWO.)
options: prim.GetAttribute("extent") returns a valid attribute although extent is not authored, because the Sphere schema defines it.
[a.GetName() for a in prim.GetAuthoredAttributes()] contains exactly "lod" and "radius".
lod.IsCustom() returns False because it has a value.
radius.GetResolveInfo().GetSource() reports a fallback value.
prim.GetAttributes() returns only lod and radius.
explanations: Schema-defined properties exist on typed prims even when nothing is authored for them.
Only those two attributes have authored opinions.
lod is declared custom and is not part of the schema, so IsCustom() is True.
radius has an authored default of 2, so the source is a default opinion, not the fallback.
GetAttributes also includes schema attributes such as extent, visibility and purpose.

questions.stem: Which prims does UsdGeomImageable.ComputeVisibility() report as invisible? (Select TWO.)
options: /World/Props/Cup
/World/Table
/World/Helper
/World/Props
explanations: visibility is inherited: an invisible ancestor makes every descendant invisible, even one that authors "inherited".
Nothing above or on Table is invisible.
purpose = guide does not change visibility; it only lets renderers include or exclude the prim by purpose (guides are usually drawn only when enabled).
It authors visibility = invisible itself.

questions.stem: A script scaled the points of /Plate but left extent untouched. Which code correctly refreshes the extent?

usda.plate.usda:
#usda 1.0

def Mesh "Plate"
{
    float3[] extent = [(-1, 0, -1), (1, 0, 1)]
    int[] faceVertexCounts = [4]
    int[] faceVertexIndices = [0, 1, 2, 3]
    point3f[] points = [(-3, 0, -2), (3, 0, -2), (3, 0, 2), (-3, 0, 2)]
}

options: mesh.GetExtentAttr().Set(UsdGeom.Boundable.ComputeExtentFromPlugins(mesh, Usd.TimeCode.Default()))
mesh.GetExtentAttr().Set(mesh.GetPointsAttr().Get())
mesh.GetExtentAttr().Clear(), since USD re-authors extent automatically whenever points change
stage.Reload()
explanations: This computes the bounds of the current points, [(-3, 0, -2), (3, 0, 2)] here, and authors them.
extent is a two-element array (min and max corners), not a copy of the points.

USD never re-authors extent when points change. Clear() only removes the authored value: extent.Get() then returns None, and UsdGeom.BBoxCache has to fall back to computing bounds from the points, which can be expensive. Author the recomputed extent instead.
Reload re-reads layers from disk and throws away unsaved edits.

questions.stem: With the stage's default (linear) interpolation, what does Get(5) return for the two attributes on Gauge? (Select TWO.)
options: needle returns 5.0
needle returns 0.0
ticks returns 0
Both return 10
ticks returns 5
explanations: Floating-point values are interpolated linearly between samples.
That would need held interpolation, which is not the default.
Integer values cannot be interpolated, so the earlier sample is held.
No type snaps to the next sample.
Linear interpolation only applies to floating-point based types.

questions.stem: What does Door.angle return at time 30 and at time 6?
options: No value at either time, because both lie outside the sampled range
135 at time 30 and -45 at time 6, by extrapolation
The default value, because time samples only apply within their range
90 at time 30 and 0 at time 6, because values are held beyond the first and last samples
explanations: A value is still returned; it is held from the nearest sample.
Time samples are never extrapolated.
No default is authored, and samples apply at all times.
Outside the sampled range, time samples clamp to the nearest sample.

questions.stem: shot.usda sublayers light_rig.usda and list-edits the lights relationship. What does GetTargets() return for /World/Rig.lights?
options: [/World/Rim, /World/Key]
[/World/Key, /World/Rim]
[/World/Rim]
[/World/Key, /World/Fill, /World/Rim]
explanations: append adds to the end; prepend would add to the front.
List edits from the stronger layer apply on top of the weaker explicit list: Fill is deleted and Rim is appended.
That would require the stronger layer to author an explicit list.
The delete operation removes Fill.

questions.stem: Which statements about attribute variability are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: xformOpOrder is declared as a uniform token[] attribute.
A uniform attribute is meant to hold one value for all time, so it should not be time-sampled.
uniform means the value is shared by every instance of a prototype.
Only array-valued attributes may be declared uniform.
Varying attributes cannot have a default value.
explanations: The op order cannot be animated; only the op values can.
uniform declares that the value does not vary over time; tools and schemas rely on that.
Variability is about time, not instancing.
Scalars can be uniform too, for example purpose or orientation.
Any attribute can have a default value in addition to time samples.

questions.stem: Where does the origin of /Arm end up in world space?

usda.arm.usda:
#usda 1.0

def Xform "Arm"
{
    float xformOp:rotateZ = 90
    double3 xformOp:translate = (2, 0, 0)
    uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:rotateZ", "xformOp:translate"]
}

explanations: A positive rotateZ turns +X toward +Y, not toward -Y.
That ignores the rotation, as if translate were listed first.
Ops apply to points from the last entry of xformOpOrder to the first: the origin is translated to (2, 0, 0) and then rotated 90 degrees about Z to (0, 2, 0).
That would be a 180-degree rotation.

questions.stem: For the layer below, which statements about UsdGeom.PrimvarsAPI(prim).FindPrimvarWithInheritance("displayColor") are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: For /Car/Trim/Strip it returns the red primvar from /Car, skipping Trim.
For /Car/Wheel it returns the red constant primvar authored on /Car.
For /Car/Trim/Strip it returns Trim's uniform primvar, because the nearest ancestor always wins.
For /Car/Trim/Strip it returns no primvar: Trim's value is not constant, so it cannot be inherited, and it also stops the search before /Car.
Inheritance works for any interpolation, as long as the ancestor's array has a single element.
explanations: The search does not skip Trim: an ancestor's authored primvar of the same name ends the search.
Wheel authors no value of its own, and the nearest ancestor value is constant, so it is inherited.
Only constant primvars are inheritable; a uniform primvar on an ancestor is never handed down.
A non-constant primvar on an ancestor blocks inheritance of that name for its descendants.
Interpolation, not array length, decides inheritability: only constant primvars inherit.

questions.stem: An exporter meant to make Box red, but viewers draw it in their default gray. What is wrong with the layer below?
options: Cube prims cannot carry a display color.
color3f is the wrong type; display colors must be float3[].
The color is on a custom attribute named displayColor, not on primvars:displayColor.
A display color needs vertex interpolation to show up on a cube.
explanations: Every Gprim, Cube included, has the primvars:displayColor primvar in its schema.
displayColor is declared as color3f[]; the value type is fine.

Primvars are attributes in the primvars: namespace, and renderers read primvars:displayColor, which is still unauthored. Author it instead (for example with UsdGeom.Gprim(prim).CreateDisplayColorAttr()).
A single value with constant interpolation (the default) colors the whole surface.

questions.stem: A skinning tool stores three float weights for every point of a 100-point mesh as one vertex-interpolated primvar. Which authoring is correct?
options: float[] primvars:weights with 300 values, interpolation = "vertex" and elementSize = 3
float[] primvars:weights with 100 values and interpolation = "vertex"; USD repeats each value three times
float[] primvars:weights with 300 values and interpolation = "faceVarying"
float3[] primvars:weights with 300 values and interpolation = "vertex"
explanations: elementSize says how many consecutive array entries belong to one interpolation element, so 100 points x 3 = 300 values. In Python: UsdGeom.PrimvarsAPI(mesh).CreatePrimvar("weights", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.FloatArray, UsdGeom.Tokens.vertex, 3).
Values are never repeated implicitly; 100 floats hold only one weight per point.
faceVarying means one element per face-vertex, which is unrelated to three weights per point.
300 float3 values are 900 numbers. (One float3 per point, 100 values, would be a different but valid layout.)

questions.stem: Which statements about role value types such as color3f, point3f, normal3f, vector3f and texCoord2f are correct? (Select THREE.)
options: color3f and float3 hold the same underlying data (a GfVec3f); the role tells tools how to interpret it, for example as a color.
point3f values are stored in double precision, while vector3f values are stored as floats.
Roles matter when geometry is transformed: points take the full transform including translation, vectors ignore translation, and normals use the inverse transpose.
Roles are lost when a layer is saved as .usdc.
normal3f values are normalized to unit length automatically when they are set.
texCoord2f is a GfVec2f with the TextureCoordinate role; float2 could hold the same numbers but loses that hint.
explanations: Sdf value types pair a C++ type with an optional role; color3f is GfVec3f with the Color role.
Both are GfVec3f (single precision); point3d and vector3d are the double-precision variants.
That is why positions, velocities and normals are declared with different roles even though they share a type.
The full type name, role included, is stored in both encodings.
USD stores the numbers you author; normalizing is up to the writer.
Some tools and renderers use the role to recognize UV sets, which is why UV primvars are usually declared texCoord2f[].

questions.stem: A digital twin places equipment in a coordinate frame whose translations reach about 6,000,000 meters, and placements must stay accurate to the millimeter. Which choice fits?
options: float3 xformOp:translate, because single precision keeps about seven significant digits
half3 xformOp:translate for compact storage
double3 xformOp:translate (the default precision for translate ops), keeping each asset's point3f data local and small
token values such as "6000000.123" so no precision is lost
explanations: Seven digits are not enough: near 6,000,000 adjacent float values are 0.5 m apart, so millimeters are lost.
half has even less precision than float.
Double precision holds millimeters at that magnitude, and keeping large offsets in transforms lets point data stay in compact, accurate float ranges.
Tokens are names, not numbers; transforms must use numeric xformOp types.

questions.stem: An exporter writes transform operations through UsdGeom.Xformable. Which statements about the value types it gets are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: AddTransformOp(PrecisionFloat) authors a compact matrix4f xformOp:transform
AddTranslateOp() defaults to double3; AddRotateXYZOp() and AddScaleOp() to float3
xformOpOrder is a varying string[] attribute listing the op names in order
All ops on one prim must share one precision, so mixing double and float fails
Precision is per op: AddTranslateOp(PrecisionFloat) gives a float3 translate
explanations: Sdf has no matrix4f type; AddTransformOp() always authors matrix4d and reports an error when PrecisionFloat is requested.
Those are the default precisions of the op-adding methods.
xformOpOrder is a uniform token[] attribute.
A double3 translate next to float3 rotate and scale ops is the common default.
Every Add...Op() method takes an optional precision argument (UsdGeom.XformOp.PrecisionFloat here); matrix ops accept only double.

questions.stem: With the stage's default linear interpolation, what do points.Get(5) and temperature.Get(5) return on the Spray prim below?
options: Both are held at their time-0 values, because arrays are never interpolated
points returns the two points authored at time 0, and temperature returns [0.5, 1.5]
points returns None at time 5, because its samples cannot be interpolated
points returns [(0, 0, 0), (0.5, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0)], and temperature returns [0.5, 1.5]
explanations: Arrays of equal length are interpolated element by element; temperature is.
Arrays whose lengths differ between the bracketing samples cannot be interpolated, so USD holds the earlier sample; temperature has two values at both times and interpolates linearly.
USD falls back to held interpolation rather than returning no value.
USD does not resample arrays to a common length.

questions.stem: shot.usda references pump.usda and authors assetInfo on the referencing prim. What do Usd.ModelAPI(prim).GetAssetName() and GetAssetVersion() return for /World/Pump?
options: None and "7", because the shot's assetInfo replaces the asset's dictionary
"Pump" and "6", because assetInfo always comes from the asset's own layer
An error, because assetInfo may only be authored in the asset's root layer
"Pump" and "7": the stronger opinion replaces only the version key
explanations: assetInfo is dictionary-valued metadata and is merged key by key, so name still comes through.
The referencing layer is stronger than the referenced asset, so its version wins.
assetInfo can be authored anywhere; a shot may record the version it pinned.
Dictionary metadata composes per key: version comes from shot.usda, name and identifier from pump.usda.

questions.stem: A sensor rig records an exposure value for every frame of a capture, and downstream tools must read it at any time code. Where should that value live?
options: In a time-sampled attribute such as custom float sensor:exposure
In the prim's customData, with one key per frame such as frame_0001
In the layer's customLayerData, which supports per-frame values
In assetInfo, because it describes the capture
explanations: Metadata cannot be time-sampled; attributes are the only scene description that varies over time, and tools read them with Get(time).
customData is metadata: it has no time samples, so per-frame keys would be a fragile imitation of animation.
Layer metadata is not time-varying either.
assetInfo identifies an asset (name, version, identifier); it is not for animated data.

questions.stem: Which calls store a note as metadata on the intended object? (Select TWO.)
options: attr.SetCustomDataByKey("source", "scanner_A") to record where one attribute's values came from
prim.SetMetadata("reviewNote", "ok") with a new key, which USD registers on first use
Usd.ModelAPI(prim).SetAssetVersion("3") to add a free-form note to customData
stage.GetRootLayer().customLayerData = {"buildId": "b42"} to stamp the layer that gets saved
prim.GetAttribute("customData:note").Set("ok")
explanations: Properties carry their own customData dictionary, separate from the prim's.
Unregistered keys are rejected; free-form notes belong in customData.
That writes the version key of assetInfo, not customData.
customLayerData is layer-level metadata, the right place for facts about the file itself.
customData is metadata, not an attribute namespace; that attribute does not exist, so Set() fails.

questions.stem: shot.usda sublayers base.usda and authors wear = None on /Ball. What do wear.Get() and wear.GetResolveInfo().GetSource() report?
options: None, with Usd.ResolveInfoSourceNone: the block makes wear resolve as if no weaker value existed
0.5 and a default-value source, because None is ignored when a weaker layer has a value
0.0 from a fallback source, the zero value of float
An error, because only schema attributes can be blocked
explanations: Blocking hides every weaker default and time sample. HasAuthoredValue() is False as well, even though base.usda still holds 0.5.
None in USDA is a value block, an opinion in its own right that wins like any stronger opinion.
A custom attribute has no schema fallback, so there is nothing to fall back to.
Any attribute's value can be blocked, custom ones included.

questions.stem: shot.usda sublayers lgt_fix.usda above rig.usda. What does GetTargets() return for /World/Rig.lights and /World/Rig.filters?

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./lgt_fix.usda@,
        @./rig.usda@
    ]
)

options: lights: [/World/Key, /World/Fill] and filters: []
Both return []: declaring a relationship in a stronger layer clears it
lights: [] and filters: [/World/Gobo]
Both keep rig.usda's targets, because = None only removes the relationship from lgt_fix.usda
explanations: This swaps the effects of the two declarations in lgt_fix.usda.
A bare declaration (rel filters) authors no target list, so weaker targets pass through.
rel lights = None authors an explicitly empty target list, which wins over rig.usda's list; rel filters only declares the relationship.
= None is an opinion (an empty explicit list), not an absence of one.

questions.stem: The Ball prim below declares wear without giving it a value. Which statements are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: wear.HasAuthoredValue() is True, because the attribute is declared.
wear.IsAuthored() is True, because the layer holds a spec for the attribute.
wear.Get() returns 0.0, the zero value of float.
wear is missing from prim.GetAuthoredAttributes(), because it has no value.
wear.Get() returns None, and wear.HasValue() is False.
explanations: A declaration creates a spec with a type but no default or time samples, so there is no authored value.
IsAuthored() asks whether any layer has a spec for the property, value or not.
Without an authored value or a schema fallback there is nothing to return, so Get() gives None.
GetAuthoredAttributes() lists attributes with authored specs, so wear is included.
HasValue() also counts schema fallbacks, which custom attributes do not have.

questions.stem: A CAD exporter wrote the Bracket mesh below. In renderers that honor subdivision, its sharp corners look rounded and the part looks shrunken. Why?
options: The extent is wrong, so the renderer guesses the shape.
subdivisionScheme is not authored, so its catmullClark fallback treats the polygons as a subdivision cage.
orientation falls back to leftHanded, which smooths the normals.
A mesh without authored normals is always rendered smoothed and shrunk.
explanations: The authored extent matches the points exactly; extents affect culling and framing, not surface shape.
A cube-shaped cage smooths toward a rounded blob. Hard-surface CAD meshes should author subdivisionScheme = "none"; exporters of polygonal data should always state it explicitly.
The orientation fallback is rightHanded, and it controls winding, not smoothing.
Missing normals change shading, not the silhouette; the shrinking comes from subdivision.

questions.stem: shot.usda (meters, Y up) references robot.usda, authored in centimeters with Z up. The robot shows up 100 times too large and lying on its back. Which statements are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: USD rescales referenced layers automatically when their metersPerUnit differs, so the size problem must come from the DCC.
Composition does not convert units or axes. The stage uses the root layer's metersPerUnit and upAxis, so Head's translate of 180 is read as 180 meters along Z.
Setting upAxis = "Z" on shot.usda rotates the referenced geometry into place.
metersPerUnit only affects physics, never what is rendered.
A fix is a corrective transform on /World/Robot, such as a 0.01 scale and a -90 degree rotation about X, or converting the asset when it is published.
explanations: There is no automatic conversion; a layer's unit and axis metadata are only descriptions.
The composed world translation of Head is (0, 0, 180) in a meters, Y-up stage.
upAxis is metadata for tools and cameras; changing it moves no geometry.
It states the length of one scene unit for all geometry and transforms, so importers, physics and any tool that needs real-world sizes depend on it.
Scaling by 0.01 turns centimeters into meters, and rotating -90 degrees about X maps +Z onto +Y.

questions.stem: Box authors no visibility, yet it vanishes during playback. At which time codes does UsdGeom.Imageable(box).ComputeVisibility() report invisible?
options: From time 5 onward, because the visibility tokens are blended halfway between samples
Only at exactly time 10, then it reappears
Never, because Box itself authors no visibility
From time 10 onward, because token samples are held and Box inherits Rig's visibility
explanations: Tokens cannot be blended; they are held.
After the last sample the value is held, so it stays invisible.
Visibility is inherited: an invisible ancestor hides the whole subtree.
Non-numeric types use held interpolation, so Rig stays inherited until 10 and is invisible from then on; ComputeVisibility() walks the ancestors at each time.

questions.stem: A script replaced the Tile mesh's points and must now author a correct extent. Which value should it write?

usda.tile.usda:
#usda 1.0

def Mesh "Tile"
{
    float3[] extent = [(0, 0, 0), (1, 1, 0)]
    int[] faceVertexCounts = [4]
    int[] faceVertexIndices = [0, 1, 2, 3]
    point3f[] points = [(-1, -1, 0), (1, -1, 0), (1, 1, 0), (-1, 1, 0)]
    double3 xformOp:translate = (10, 0, 0)
    uniform token[] xformOpOrder = ["xformOp:translate"]
}

options: [(-1, -1, 0), (1, 1, 0)], the bounds of the points in local space
[(9, -1, 0), (11, 1, 0)], including the prim's own translate
[(-1, -1, -1), (1, 1, 1)], because an extent must be a cube
The eight corners of the tile's bounding box
explanations: Extent is measured in the prim's local space, before its own xformOps. UsdGeom.Boundable.ComputeExtentFromPlugins(mesh, time) returns exactly this; BBoxCache applies transforms later.
That is the world-space bound; extent excludes the prim's own transform.
An extent is a box, not a cube; a flat tile has zero depth.
extent is a two-element float3[]: the minimum and maximum corners.

questions.stem: After moving the points of the Dots prim below, a script refreshes its extent with UsdGeom.Boundable.ComputeExtentFromPlugins(). Which extent does it compute?
options: [(0, 0, 0), (2, 0, 0)], the bounds of the point positions only
[(-0.5, -0.5, -0.5), (2.5, 0.5, 0.5)], padding every point by the largest radius
[(-0.5, -1, -1), (3, 1, 1)], padding each point by its full width
[(-0.25, -0.5, -0.5), (2.5, 0.5, 0.5)]: each point is padded by half its own width
explanations: Points are drawn as spheres or discs of the given width, so their extent must include that size.
The computation pads each point by its own radius, so the first point only reaches -0.25 in x.
widths are diameters; the padding is half the width.
Point 0 extends 0.25 and point 1 extends 0.5 in every direction; the box encloses both.

questions.stem: The Wave mesh's points are time-sampled, but its extent was authored once as a default value. Which statements are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: UsdGeom.BBoxCache at time 10 reports [(0, 0, 0), (3, 1, 2)] for Wave, because it always derives bounds from the points.
extent.Get(10) is interpolated from the points automatically.
UsdGeom.Boundable.ComputeExtentFromPlugins(mesh, Usd.TimeCode(10)) returns [(0, 0, 0), (3, 1, 2)].
The extent should be time-sampled at the same times as points, computing and setting a value for each points sample.
Renderers ignore a default-valued extent whenever points are animated.
explanations: BBoxCache trusts an authored extent, so it reports the stale [(0, 0, 0), (1, 1, 0)] and culling or framing goes wrong.
USD never derives one attribute from another; extent.Get(10) returns the authored default.
It computes the bounds from the points at that time, ignoring the authored extent.
Animated geometry needs animated extents so every frame's bound is right.
Consumers use the authored extent as given; that is why a stale one causes problems.

questions.stem: A script creates thousands of prim and property specs in a loop and is slow because the stage reacts to every single edit. Which statements about Sdf.ChangeBlock are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: It pays off most for many Sdf-level edits, such as creating thousands of specs or setting many values in a loop.
It turns the edits into an undoable transaction that rolls back if an exception occurs.
It is required for every edit made from Python.
It defers change notification until the block closes, so the stage processes one batch of changes instead of reacting to every edit.
It speeds up read-only work such as stage.Traverse().
explanations: That is exactly the case where per-edit change processing dominates the run time.
A change block provides no undo or rollback; the edits are applied either way.
Change blocks are an optional optimization.
Batching notices means recomposition and downstream listeners run once for the whole set of edits.
Reads trigger no change notifications, so there is nothing to batch.

questions.stem: An artist changed the default value of the Door's xformOp:translate to (0, 0, 5), but at frame 1 the door still sits at the origin. Why?
options: xformOpOrder must be re-authored after changing an op's value.
In this layer the attribute also has time samples, and for queries at a specific time they take precedence over the default; the default only answers queries at the Default time code.
A default value is always weaker than time samples from any layer.
double3 values cannot be authored as defaults on transform ops.
explanations: xformOpOrder only lists which ops apply; changing a value never requires touching it.
Edit or remove the time samples, or author the change in a stronger layer, to see the new value at frame 1.
Across layers, strength decides: a stronger layer's default wins over a weaker layer's time samples. The rule here concerns the same layer.
Defaults of any value type are allowed on ops.

questions.stem: yard.usda overrides wear on Crate_01's Box, but /Yard/Crate_01/Box.wear still reads 0.8. Why?
options: References are stronger than local opinions, so the referenced 0.8 wins.
Custom attributes cannot be overridden from another layer.
The over must be a def to override a referenced value.
Crate_01 is instanceable, and opinions on descendants of an instance are ignored because those descendants come from the shared prototype.
explanations: Local opinions are the strongest; the over is ignored only because of instancing.
Custom attributes compose like any other attribute.
The specifier is not the problem; the prim lives inside an instance.
Edit the instance prim itself, broadcast through a class, add an arc, or deinstance to change them.

questions.stem: A review tool opens shot.usda and then calls stage.MuteLayer() with lighting.usda's identifier. What intensity does /World/Key report?

usda.shot.usda:
#usda 1.0
(
    subLayers = [
        @./lighting.usda@,
        @./layout.usda@
    ]
)

options: No value, because muting a sublayer also mutes the layers listed after it
explanations: That is the value while lighting.usda is not muted.
Muting removes lighting.usda's opinions from composition, so layout.usda's value is the strongest one left.
Muting affects only the named layer (and anything it alone brings in).
Opinions are never summed.
